items.toString:
h3. Summary

Add an upstream Golang {{only-FIPS}} mode that ensures FIPS is enabled and does not silently fall back to non-FIPS crypto.

h3. Context

Our current FIPS implementation has a feature called “FIPS or die”.  
It ensures that FIPS is working and prevents silent fallback to non-FIPS validated crypto.

As we move to upstream Golang-based FIPS/crypto, we need the same capability.  
Upstream Golang currently has a flag for a best-effort attempt at FIPS.

h3. Acceptance criteria

* Add a flag for {{only FIPS}}.
* When {{only FIPS}} is enabled, the system must exit or die explicitly if FIPS is not enabled.
* The system must not silently fall back to non-FIPS crypto.
* Prefer an upstream solution if possible.
* If needed, carry a patch in the meantime.
* Plumb this configuration through to all Golang binaries.
* Support passing the configuration through:
** build flags and conflux, or
** runtime flags in the system

h3. Other information

* The existing feature is called “FIPS or die”.
* The upstream Golang flag currently only best-effort attempts FIPS.

items.fromString:
h3. *Feature Overview*

As part of OpenShift 5's expansion to a 5-year lifecycle with the Extended Lifecycle (ELC) concept, OpenShift Data Foundation, as a platform-aligned operator, will need to adopt this new lifecycle model accordingly. This means customers can benefit from the same yearly cadence of ELC releases, the same extended full support phase, a congruent maintenance support phase, and ELC support, providing up to 5 years of support in total. OpenShift Data Foundation will also provide an ELC SKU to purchase the support lifecycle extension as a companion to its standalone SKU.

h3. *Goals*

OpenShift Data Foundation continues to fully align with OpenShift's lifecycle as it did with EUS releases before, while adapting to the novelties of OpenShift 5. Thus, customers procuring OpenShift 5 ELC subscriptions get more value out of this offering by including OpenShift Data Foundation into the set of guarantees ELC delivers: the ability to version-lock the platform stack to a set of selected minor releases of the cluster and operators, never being forced to apply anything other than patch releases to either of them throughout a period of up to 5 years. This reduces friction for customers in consuming the OpenShift value-add by eliminating the need to plan and align fragmented lifecycle models across offerings. It also lowers the risk of breaking changes being introduced to the platform stack over up to 5 years, which would cause disruption and operational overhead. In addition, the timing of ELC releases becomes more predictable with the annual summer release.

h3. *Requirements:*

OpenShift Data Foundation aligns with OpenShift 5 ELC releases, which means:

* Once a year, OpenShift Data Foundation offers a version that offers a total of 5 years of support, with the same start and end dates for the full support (see exception below), maintenance support and ELC support phases
* The start date of the full support phase of the ELC release of OpenShift Data Foundation must not trail the corresponding OpenShift ELC release GA date by more than 2 weeks
* The scope definitions and guarantees for the full, maintenance and ELC support phases for OpenShift Data Foundation ELC releases are the same as those for OpenShift ELC releases
* OpenShift Data Foundation ELC offers 12 months of full support, followed by 12 months of maintenance support, followed by 36 months of ELC support, for a total of 5 years
* Customers are entitled to ELC support for OpenShift Data Foundation either as part of an ELC subscription for OpenShift Platform Plus or an ELC subscription specific to OpenShift Data Foundation procured as a standalone offering
* The ELC model starts with the introduction of OpenShift 5, which means, effectively, at OpenShift 5.2 GA, OpenShift Data Foundation would introduce or designate its first ELC release
* OpenShift Data Foundation will support ELC-to-ELC updates with direct skip-level updates, which means users do not need to update to intermediate versions of OpenShift Data Foundation in order to reach the next ELC release from a given ELC
* The compatibility with OpenShift releases must be either N-3 or N+3 in order to allow skip-level updates (in alignment with [OCPSTRAT-2638|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2638]), depending on whether OpenShift Data Foundation or the cluster is supposed to be updated first
* OpenShift Data Foundation's version numbering will align with OpenShift, so that OpenShift Data Foundation 5.0 will align (and release) with OpenShift 5.0, OpenShift Data Foundation 5.1 with OpenShift 5.1 etc.

h3. *Questions to Answer:*

* "What if there are breaking changes between two ELC releases of OpenShift Data Foundation?"
** While breaking changes should be avoided wherever possible (and are technically not allowed in a minor version change, even if it's a 3 minor version difference), there are rare occasions where they occur. The OpenShift Data Foundation operator needs to provide a direct update path, applying migrations wherever possible to reduce manual post-update steps, even when the resulting version introduces breaking changes.
* "Skip-level upgrades are very difficult, and we have never supported them. Is this a must-have?"
** Yes, since the benefit of skip-level update support in OpenShift would be negated by the lack of support in the platform/ELC-aligned operators. The first skip-level update that customers will be able to conduct is going to be from 5.2 to 5.5, so by mid-2028, your operator needs to support skip-level updates.

h3. *Customer Considerations*

* Customers clearly identify the ELC release of OpenShift Data Foundation in the Product Lifecycle Data [externally|https://access.redhat.com/support/policy/updates/openshift_operators] and [inside the cluster|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2618]
* Customers, as part of preparing an ELC-to-ELC cluster update, can directly update OpenShift Data Foundation from the current ELC release to the next, either before or after updating the cluster.

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

* OpenShift Data Foundation documentation and release notes need to clearly call out what the ELC-to-ELC update steps look like, plus any follow-up work the user has to conduct outside of OLM managing the operator update

items.toString:
h3. Description

Currently, the *Zero Trust Workload Identity Manager (ZTWIM)* is optimized for standard x86_64 architectures. This feature extends ZTWIM support to *ARM64 architecture*, enabling customers to natively run the identity manager on ARM64-based cluster nodes and instances. 

h3.  Business Case & Value

* *Cost Optimization:* Infrastructure teams are actively migrating workloads to *Cloud instances such as AWS Graviton (ARM64)*, instances to take advantage of better price-to-performance ratios.
* *Customer Impact:* Providing ARM64 support allows our customers to significantly lower their Cloud compute costs while maintaining their zero-trust security posture.

h3. Acceptance Criteria

To consider this feature complete, the following must be achieved:

# *Successful Deployment:* ZTWIM must successfully deploy and initialize on ARM64 nodes (e.g., AWS Graviton EC2 instances or EKS ARM64 node groups).
# *Functional Parity:* All core features of ZTWIM (identity issuance, token validation, etc.) must function identically to the x86_64 version with no performance regressions.
# *Documentation Update:* Update installation guides and system requirements to officially list ARM64/Graviton as a supported architecture.

h3. Technical Notes / Considerations

*Note for Development:* Review the {{ZTWIM}} codebase for any hardcoded x86_64 base images, architecture-specific binaries, or low-level dependencies that will need to be swapped or multi-compiled for ARM64.
This work item is documented by OSDOCS-20570

items.fromString:
*Feature Overview*

* *Default-on* GOMAXPROCS=1 for all platform pods in OpenShift 5.0
* Zero-touch remediation with opt-out safety valve
* Eliminates GC latency spikes and thread proliferation on high-core-count nodes



  *Goals & Outcomes*

* Platform pod thread count reduction: 130+ → <40 (75%+ reduction)
* GC p99 latency: 1000ms → <200ms (80%+ improvement)
* API timeout rate: 5-10% → <1% (50%+ reduction)
* Zero customer action required



  *Requirements*

* *Functional*: Default injection, opt-out API, automatic upgrade behavior
* *Non-Functional*: Security, performance targets, reliability, compatibility



  *Use Cases*

# New cluster deployment on 256-core infrastructure
# Fleet upgrade from 4.x → 5.0 (automatic optimization)
# Opt-out for edge case HPC workloads



  *Open Questions for Engineering*

* GOMAXPROCS=1 vs dynamic value?
* Opt-out API design (CRD, ConfigMap, MachineConfig)?
* Scope: only openshift-* namespaces or broader?
* How to handle existing manual 4.x MachineConfigs during upgrade?



  *Success Metrics*

  ▎ _95% adoption (clusters with optimization active)_

* <5% opt-out rate
* Performance improvements validated via telemetry
* -90% reduction in GOMAXPROCS-related support cases



  *Risk Assessment*

* Includes mitigation strategies for workload regression, opt-out API reliability, upgrade behavior

items.fromString:
h2. Vision

Shift engineering time from typing code to the work that actually requires human judgment:

* *Deciding what to build:* prioritization, product direction
* *Design discussions:* architecture, API contracts, trade-offs
* *Reliability engineering:* making it production grade and scalable
* *Cost visibility:* understanding the dollar cost per feature delivered

h2. Goals

Organically grow into a framework that decouples distributed consumption of reusable building blocks (skills, slash, agents, knowledge...) from a centralized system that orchestrates llm execution at scale and that enable flexible implementation choices (like ambient or the agent CI workflow).

h2. Building blocks

* Discuss design / implementation plan with claude interactive session
* /jira:create
* /jira:generate-test-plan
* /jira:solve
* /code-review:pr /code-review:pre-commit-review
* /agentic-qe test-plan
* /address-review

h2. Proposal

Enable scaffolding for devs to leverage the building blocks for Discovery and Delivery locally as choice in their workflows.

Integrate the building blocks with automated CI on PRs for dogfooding, centralized gating and result tracking.

Integrate the building blocks as impl details pre PR of the Agent Workflow.

h2. CI Agent Workflow

h2. Phase 1: Prototype

Established a reusable foundational pipeline and building blocks for AI-assisted development:

* */jira:solve:* a skill that takes a Jira issue, analyzes the codebase, implements a fix, and opens a draft PR
* *Jira label-driven automation:* tag an issue with {{issue-for-agent}}, and a periodic CI job picks it up, solves it, reviews its own output, and creates a PR
* *CI plumbing:* proved the model works at scale through Prow periodic jobs with artifact collection and per-run HTML reports

h2. Phase 2: Quality & Accessibility

Shift from useful prototype to business impact by raising quality:

* *Multi-phase pipeline:* Solve → Review → Fix review findings → PR creation → Address PR review comments automatically
* *Feedback loops:*
** Systematically exercise the pipeline across a backlog of issues, using pass rates and review findings to tune prompts, skills, and agent behavior
** Democratize triggering: make it accessible beyond CI via Slack commands and kubectl-based triggers, so any team member can kick off a solve
* *Prompt tracking and cost visibility:* track and report token usage, API cost, and duration per issue, per phase. Surface cost-per-feature metrics so the team can make informed decisions about what's worth automating. Example report [https://gcsweb-ci.apps.ci.l2s4.p1.openshiftapps.com/gcs/test-platform-results/pr-logs/pull/openshift_release/74809/rehearse-74809-periodic-ci-openshift-hypershift-main-periodic-jira-agent/2025198575218069504/artifacts/periodic-jira-agent/hypershift-jira-agent-report/artifacts/jira-agent-report.html|https://gcsweb-ci.apps.ci.l2s4.p1.openshiftapps.com/gcs/test-platform-results/pr-logs/pull/openshift_release/74809/rehearse-74809-periodic-ci-openshift-hypershift-main-periodic-jira-agent/2025198575218069504/artifacts/periodic-jira-agent/hypershift-jira-agent-report/artifacts/jira-agent-report.html]
* *Quality gating:* build confidence metrics (CI pass rate, review verdict, human edits post-merge) to measure how close the output is to merge-ready

h2. Phase 3: Agent as Default Workflow

The pipeline handles the majority of routine implementation work:

* 80% of routine coding is done by the pipeline: bug fixes, boilerplate features, test additions, API wiring
* Engineers review, refine, and merge: the human role shifts to approval, design guidance, and handling the 20% that requires deep context and more iterative local pipelines

h2. Vision

Shift engineering time from typing code to the work that actually requires human judgment:

* *Deciding what to build:* prioritization, product direction
* *Design discussions:* architecture, API contracts, trade-offs
* *Reliability engineering:* making it production grade and scalable
* *Cost visibility:* understanding the dollar cost per feature delivered

h2. Goals

Grow into a framework that enables reusable building blocks (skills, slash, agents, knowledge...) by multiple consumption models. Specifically:

OCPbug autofix platform - via automated prow jobs

Developer laptop - executable chained workflows

Slack - Chai-bot

h2. Building blocks

* Discuss design / implementation plan with claude interactive session
* /jira:create
* /jira:generate-test-plan
* /jira:solve
* /code-review:pr /code-review:pre-commit-review
* /address
* /agentic-qe test-plan
* /address-review

h2. Proposal

Enable distribution of a common bundle e.g. claude plugin

Adopt the plugin in the hypershift ocpbug autofix platform.

Scale the platform to other teams

Enable dev laptop use case

h2. CI Agent Workflow

h2. Phase 1: Prototype

Established a reusable foundational pipeline and building blocks for AI-assisted development:

* */jira:solve, others:* a skill that takes a Jira issue, analyzes the codebase, implements a fix, and opens a draft PR
* *Jira label-driven automation:* tag an issue with {{issue-for-agent}}, and a periodic CI job picks it up, solves it, reviews its own output, and creates a PR
* *CI plumbing:* proved the model works at scale through Prow periodic jobs with artifact collection and per-run HTML reports

h2. Phase 2: Quality & Accessibility

Shift from useful prototype to business impact by raising quality:

* *Multi-phase pipeline:* Solve → Review → Fix review findings → PR creation → Address PR review comments automatically
* *Feedback loops:*
** Systematically exercise the pipeline across a backlog of issues, using pass rates and review findings to tune prompts, skills, and agent behavior
** Democratize triggering: make it accessible beyond CI via Slack commands and kubectl-based triggers, so any team member can kick off a solve

Surface cost-per-feature metrics so the team can make informed decisions about what's worth automating. h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*

Shift engineering time from typing code to the work that actually requires human judgment — prioritization, architecture, design trade-offs, and reliability engineering — by establishing an AI-assisted development platform that automates routine coding tasks across the OpenShift development lifecycle.

The platform provides reusable building blocks (skills, slash commands, agents, domain knowledge) consumed through multiple interfaces: CI automation (Prow periodic jobs), developer laptops (interactive Claude Code sessions), and team collaboration (Slack via Chai-bot). It enables a multi-phase pipeline — Solve → Review → Fix → PR creation → Address review comments — that handles bug fixes, boilerplate features, test additions, and API wiring with minimal human intervention.

This is an internal engineering productivity initiative that does not change the OpenShift product itself, but fundamentally transforms how it is developed by targeting 80% automation of routine implementation work while engineers shift to approval, design guidance, and handling the 20% that requires deep context.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

* *Automated issue resolution:* Engineers tag a Jira issue with {{issue-for-agent}}, and a periodic CI job picks it up, implements a fix, reviews its own output, and creates a PR — no human coding required for routine issues
* *Multi-phase quality pipeline:* Solve → self-review → fix findings → PR creation → automated response to PR review comments, producing merge-ready output
* *Reusable building blocks:* A distributable skill/agent bundle (Claude plugin) enabling consistent agentic workflows across teams and consumption models
* *Cost visibility:* Per-issue, per-phase tracking of token usage, API cost, and duration, surfacing cost-per-feature metrics so teams can make informed decisions about what to automate
* *Cross-team scalability:* Modular CI plumbing (Prow jobs, step registry refs) that other OpenShift teams can adopt without reimplementing the infrastructure

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)*

# A Prow periodic job MUST pick up Jira issues labeled {{issue-for-agent}}, implement a fix, and open a draft PR with an HTML report artifact
# The pipeline MUST execute a multi-phase workflow: solve, self-review, fix review findings, PR creation, and address reviewer comments
# Skills and agents MUST be distributable as a common bundle (Claude plugin) usable across CI, developer laptops, and Slack
# Per-issue telemetry MUST track and report token usage, API cost, duration, and phase-level breakdown
# Quality gating MUST include measurable confidence metrics: CI pass rate, review verdict, and post-merge human edit rate
# The platform MUST support sandboxed execution of agentic workloads in CI to prevent unintended side effects
# Eval and regression CI MUST systematically exercise the pipeline across a backlog of issues to measure and improve pass rates

*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed. Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios._*

||Deployment considerations||List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)||
|Self-managed, managed, or both|N/A — internal engineering tooling, does not ship as product|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|N/A|
|Hosted control planes|N/A|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all|N/A|
|Connected / Restricted Network|CI infrastructure requires network access to LLM API endpoints|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_64 (CI infrastructure)|
|Operator compatibility|N/A|
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|N/A|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|N/A|
|Other (please specify)|Requires Anthropic API access for Claude models in CI and developer environments|

h3. *Use Cases (Optional)*

* *Automated bug fix:* An engineer triages a bug, adds the {{issue-for-agent}} label, and receives a draft PR within the next CI cycle without writing any code
* *Interactive development:* A developer uses Claude Code locally with the shared skill bundle to discuss design, generate test plans, implement features, and self-review before pushing
* *Slack-driven workflows:* A team lead asks Chai-bot to summarize CI health, generate a feature status report, or kick off a solve for a specific issue
* *Cross-team adoption:* Another OpenShift team configures the modular Prow job and skill bundle for their repository, gaining agentic development capabilities without building their own infrastructure

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional)*

* What guardrails are needed for agentic workloads that modify code in CI (sandboxing, resource limits, secret access)?
* How should cost budgets be managed per team or per issue type to prevent runaway spending?
* What is the minimum quality bar (CI pass rate, review verdict) for promoting agent output from draft to ready-for-review?

h3. *Out of Scope*

* Changes to the OpenShift product itself — this is purely internal engineering tooling
* General-purpose AI/ML platform capabilities for OpenShift customers
* Automated merging without human approval — the agent creates PRs, humans merge

h3. *Background*

The HyperShift / Control Planes team has been developing this platform since early 2026 under [CNTRLPLANE-2791|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/CNTRLPLANE-2791]. The work has progressed through three phases:

* *Phase 1 (Prototype):* Established foundational pipeline — /jira:solve skill, Jira label-driven automation, CI plumbing via Prow periodic jobs
* *Phase 2 (Quality & Accessibility):* Multi-phase pipeline with feedback loops, cost tracking, quality gating, and democratized access via Slack and developer laptops
* *Phase 3 (Agent as Default Workflow):* Target state where the pipeline handles 80% of routine implementation, with engineers reviewing and merging

Key child epics under active development include: common skills bundle distribution (CNTRLPLANE-3677), modular Prow job for cross-team reuse (CNTRLPLANE-3674), OTEL observability (CNTRLPLANE-3680), eval/CI for the solve workflow (CNTRLPLANE-3679), agentic QE (CNTRLPLANE-3681), and sandboxing for CI workloads (CNTRLPLANE-3750).

h3. *Customer Considerations*

This is an internal engineering initiative. Indirect customer benefit comes from faster bug resolution, higher code quality through systematic AI-assisted review, and increased engineering capacity redirected toward reliability and feature work.

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

* Agentic SDLC framework documented at [docs/content/how-to/agentic-sdlc.md|https://github.com/openshift/hypershift/blob/main/docs/content/how-to/agentic-sdlc.md]
* Cross-team adoption guide needed for the modular Prow job and skill bundle

h3. *Interoperability Considerations*

* Depends on Anthropic Claude API availability for CI and developer workstations
* Integrates with OpenShift CI (Prow), Jira Cloud, GitHub, and Slack
* The modular skill bundle targets adoption by other OpenShift engineering teams (networking, storage, installer, etc.)

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

_Service mesh should support skipping Istio versions during an upgrade for the following reasons:_

* Most OpenShift Service Mesh customers do not upgrade more than once or twice per year, thus it is advantageous for them to be able to upgrade more easily across multiple versions of Istio (up to 4 releases).
* Several customers have delayed upgrading to Service Mesh 3, thus if they are coming from Service Mesh 2.6, it is advantageous to upgrade to the latest release of Service Mesh 3 with as few steps as possible.
* OSSM is being asked to support skip-level upgrades as part of the OCP 5 extended support ([https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3372|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3372|smart-link]  )

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

* Provide a path for users to upgrade across multiple releases of Istio(e.g. Istio 1.30 → 1.34) with a single step:
** For proxies (incl. ztunnel), a single restart to jump versions 
** For ambient mode, a single ztunnel restart
** For sidecar mode, a single application pod restart

This should be done while maintaining application availability and not interrupting service traffic wherever possible. If there is a known potential service interruption, it should be noted. The administrative work to achieve such a migration should be minimized - and automated by Istio and/or the OSSM operator where possible.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

_A list of specific needs or objectives that a feature must deliver in order to be considered complete.  Be sure to include nonfunctional requirements such as security, reliability, performance, maintainability, scalability, usability, etc._  {color:#0747a6}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

_Created with AI assistance._

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

OSSM customers upgrade (on average) once per year. Istio releases a new minor version roughly every quarter. This means a customer returning to upgrade after a year may need to traverse *up to 3 OSSM operator/product releases and 4 Istio minor versions* to reach the current release.

Istio's current upgrade model enforces an *N-1 version skew* between the control plane and data plane — meaning a customer at Istio 1.30 must upgrade sequentially through 1.31, 1.32, 1.33 before reaching 1.34. Each hop is a separate operator update and workload restart cycle. This is difficult for administrators who may have to coordinate both Istio control plane updates and workload restarts across a large number of teams.

Three drivers motivate this feature:

# *Customer upgrade behaviour.* Most customers do not upgrade more than once or twice per year. Requiring 3–4 sequential hops to stay current is a significant operational burden that discourages upgrades entirely, leaving customers on older, less secure versions.
# *OSSM 2.6 → 3.x migration tail.* Customers who recently migrated from OSSM 2.6 to 3.0 want to reach the latest 3.x release (e.g. 3.4) without another multi-step upgrade cycle so soon after their initial migration.
# *OCP 5 Extended Update Support.* OCPSTRAT-3372 establishes EUS for OCP 5. Service mesh must support skip-level upgrades to match the platform's EUS lifecycle, so customers upgrading between EUS releases can update OSSM in a single maintenance window.

This feature delivers a supported path for upgrading OSSM across *up to 4 Istio minor versions* (e.g. 1.30 → 1.34) with a single administrative action.



h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

# With the OSSM operator, a cluster administrator updates the {{Istio}} CR to the target version once. The sail-operator handles all intermediate steps without further manual intervention.
# Application availability is maintained wherever possible. Any disruption windows are documented with expected duration and blast radius.
# *Sidecar mode:* One rolling restart of application pods completes the data plane upgrade.
# *Ambient mode:* One ztunnel update completes L4; waypoints require at most one rollout restart.
# *Pre-flight validation* catches blockers (deprecated APIs, incompatible EnvoyFilters, missing images, Kubernetes version mismatch) before any in-cluster state is modified.
# The upgrade works in both connected and disconnected/restricted network environments.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

* The sail-operator is able to update up to 3 OSSM versions (one year) in a single administrative step 
* The Istio CRD is able to update itself up to 4 Istio minor versions (one year) ahead of the installed version and begins the upgrade without requiring multiple administrator-initiated CR edits (if no issues).
* A Pre-flight validation runs before any in-cluster mutation. Blocking errors report the specific resource and remediation action in {{.status.conditions}}. E.g. Envoy Filter creates risk. Warnings allow the upgrade to proceed but remain visible.
* If the upgrade internally requires intermediate version hops (due to the N-1 constraint), the operator performs them automatically and reports progress via the {{Istio}} CR {{.status}}.
* The upgrade is validated on all supported architectures: x86_64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), IBM Z (s390x).
* The upgrade works in disconnected environments using mirrored images; no internet access is required at upgrade time.
* The supported skip window is validated against the OCP 5 EUS release cadence (OCPSTRAT-3372) to confirm it covers the full EUS-to-EUS upgrade span.
* A multi-cluster upgrade sequence is documented, with the supported inter-cluster version skew during the upgrade window defined and tested. 

*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both| both|
|Classic (standalone cluster)| Y|
|Hosted control planes| Y|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all| Y (Momentary disruption necessary on SNO due)|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Both|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)| Y|
|Operator compatibility| servicemeshoperator3 (sail-operator)|
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|No|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)| No, CR status is source of truth. Kiali may be helpful for monitoring large mesh upgrades.|
|Other (please specify)| |

h3. 

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*

h3. 1. Orchestrated intermediate hops vs. extended xDS backward compatibility

Two valid approaches:

*(A) Operator-orchestrated sequential hops.* The sail-operator steps through intermediate versions (1.30→1.31→...→1.34), keeping each individual hop within the N-1 policy. No upstream Istio changes required to the xDS compatibility layer. The administrator triggers a single CR update; the operator executes the sequence internally. Trade-offs: more complex operator state machine; intermediate CRD migrations must be applied in order; failure recovery at mid-sequence is non-trivial; possibly slower.

*(B) Extended upstream xDS backward compatibility.* Upstream Istio extends its supported skew so a 1.34 istiod can serve 1.30 proxies. Requires upstream contribution, community agreement, and testing across the full compatibility matrix. Trade-offs: simpler operator (single hop), faster upgrade; but significant upstream effort and the community may not accept N-4 as a supported target.

A hybrid is also possible — e.g. extend upstream to N-2 and have the operator do 2-hop sequences for N-4 — but the baseline decision between these two philosophies must be made first.

h3. 2. Istio API deprecation boundaries

Istio periodically removes API versions (e.g. [networking.istio.io/v1alpha3|http://networking.istio.io/v1alpha3]). A 4-version skip may cross a removal boundary. Options: (a) the operator pre-flight check blocks on deprecated resources and requires the user to migrate them first, (b) the operator auto-migrates resources, (c) the operator warns but proceeds. A policy decision is needed, and the pre-flight check must implement it.



h3. *Out of Scope*

* *OSSM 2.6 → 3.x migration* — API resource migration ({{SMCP}}/{{SMMR}} → {{Istio}}/{{IstioRevision}}); assume user is on OSSM 3.0+.
* *Kubernetes version skip-level* — Kubernetes version requirements are a constraint to document, not an OSSM feature to implement
* *Automated downgrade* — Istio does not support downgrade; recovery from a failed upgrade is documented, not automated
* *EnvoyFilter auto-remediation* — the operator warns on incompatible filters but does not rewrite them (pre-flight validation)
* *UI changes* (OpenShift Console, OCM) — status via {{Istio}} CR only
* *Kiali* — separate lifecycle; not in scope, though Revision monitoring features may be useful.
* *Cross-cluster coordinated upgrades* — each cluster upgrades independently

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

This will require additional procedures in the OpenShift Service Mesh: [https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_service_mesh/3.3/html/updating/index|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_openshift_service_mesh/3.3/html/updating/index|smart-link] for each epic:

* *Sidecar mode (GA / OSSM-14856):* Full OSSM product documentation — upgrade procedure, pre-flight reference, EnvoyFilter guidance, multi-cluster sequence, disconnected image staging, rollback/recovery. See OSSM-14856 for the complete list.
* *Ambient mode (DP / OSSM-14857):* Upstream Istio and sail-operator documentation is the primary deliverable. OSSM docs limited to release notes and known limitations. See OSSM-14857.

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Extend the {{ClusterImagePolicy}} and {{ImagePolicy}} APIs to allow declaring deny-by-default policies.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

Currently, the default policy on OpenShift machines [is |https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blob/88815d398884bae3aa3d2d312a8897865f3d383b/templates/master/01-master-container-runtime/_base/files/policy.yaml#L8][_insecureAcceptAnything_|https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blob/88815d398884bae3aa3d2d312a8897865f3d383b/templates/master/01-master-container-runtime/_base/files/policy.yaml#L8].  Current {{ClusterImagePolicy}} and {{ImagePolicy}} APIs allow OCP and cluster admins to say “for pullspecs like _$PREFIX_, require Sigstore signatures by _$KEY_”.  This feature is asking for a new image policy OpenShift API knob to set the default policy for machines to deny.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

CRI-O and other containers/image consumers [already support|https://github.com/containers/image/blob/df7e80d2d19872b61f352a8a182ec934dc0c2346/docs/containers-policy.json.5.md#a-reasonably-locked-down-system] {{"default": [{"type": "reject"}]}}, the missing pieces are just:

* Extending [_scopes_|https://github.com/openshift/api/blob/b56324c0aed501e3ef058836f2da2af0d13d8ab8/config/v1/types_image_policy.go#L36-L50] to allow saying “I’m talking about the default scope”.
* Extending [_policy_|https://github.com/openshift/api/blob/b56324c0aed501e3ef058836f2da2af0d13d8ab8/config/v1/types_image_policy.go#L51-L54] to allow saying “reject”.
* Wiring those new API knobs up to [the machine-config operator’s existing logic for setting default-reject|https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blame/88815d398884bae3aa3d2d312a8897865f3d383b/pkg/controller/container-runtime-config/helpers.go#L625], which is currently only set [when an image-mirror config sets allowed registries|https://github.com/openshift/machine-config-operator/blob/88815d398884bae3aa3d2d312a8897865f3d383b/pkg/controller/container-runtime-config/container_runtime_config_controller.go#L1392] (I think; I could be misreading the current MCO code).
* A test case adding an ImagePolicy with the new configuration to a test Namespace, and confirming that an attempt to launch a Pod with a container referencing a local-cluster-registry image fails on the lack of a trusted signature.

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both|both|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|yes|
|Hosted control planes|yes, although [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-78297|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-78297|smart-link] menas HyperShift currently doesn’t care about (Cluster)ImagePolicy|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all|all|
|Connected / Restricted Network|both|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|all|
|Operator compatibility|n/a|
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|no|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|no|
|Other (please specify)| |

h3. *Customer Considerations*

Docs should probably point out that setting a default-deny ClusterImagePolicy will break the ability to run OLM-catalogs and other images that don’t have covering ClusterImagePolicies yet (getting those policies set up is tracked in [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3214|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3214|smart-link] ).

h2. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary).*      

+*Phase-2 Feature is for incomplete epics of*+ +*OCPSTRAT-2484*+

This feature aims to improve the user experience for cluster upgrades by providing more accurate and reliable status information for Cluster Operators. 
To ensure that operators behave predictably during upgrades and other cluster lifecycle events, and thus reduce confusion about the upgrade process.
This will be achieved by enforcing new rules for operator behavior and tracking compliance to address common issues reported by customers.

A successful upgrade path for a given {{ClusterOperator}} should follow a specific pattern:

# Before Upgrade starts, Operators are in a healthy, stable state: {{Available=True}}, {{Progressing=False}}, {{Degraded=False}}.

# When Upgrade starts the operator should become {{Progressing=True}} as it works to apply the new version.
It should *not* become {{Degraded=True}} or {{Available=False}}.

# After Upgrade, the operator should return to a state of {{Progressing=False}}, with {{Available=True}} and {{Degraded=False}}.



h2. Overall Bug Tracker

||Count||Bugs||
|14|[+OCPBUGS-20056+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-20056], [+OCPBUGS-23746+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-23746], [+OCPBUGS-38661+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38661], [+OCPBUGS-38662+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38662], [+OCPBUGS-38663+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38663], [+OCPBUGS-38678+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38678], [+OCPBUGS-62629+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62629], [+OCPBUGS-62633+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62633], [+OCPBUGS-63116+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-63116], [+OCPBUGS-65896+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65896], [+OCPBUGS-65984+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65984], [+OCPBUGS-66027+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66027], [+OCPBUGS-66213+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66213], [+OCPBUGS-86308+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-86308]|

h2. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

As a cluster-admin I want to get accurate information about the status of cluster operators and monitor the upgrade process without encountering false alarms.

* ClusterOperator must not report Degrade=True or Available=False during the course of a normal upgrade. OCP bugs haven been filed in this area [1].
* Operators MUST go progressing when transitioning between versions (We will need to decide how to enforce it. Ideas are [here|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJ1J9C3V4/p1758557182452289?thread_ts=1758555726.800399&cid=CJ1J9C3V4]). For now, this goal applies only to HA clusters.
* Operators MUST NOT re-enter progressing state when simply observing node lifecycle events such as scaleup/scaledown or reboots – primarily an issue for operators that observe DaemonSets continuously: bugs coming from OTA-1637.
* OCP bugs will be filed for the cluster operator that take too long to upgrade OTA-1626.

Eventually, with these changes we should have Accurate status reporting, clear and clean upgrade progress information, Stable Operator status

* The bugs in a single Jira query grouped by Component: [Bugs causing false alarms in ClusterOperator status during OpenShift upgrades|https://redhat.atlassian.net/issues/?filter=12483797]
* The bugs in JIRA Dashboard: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|smart-link]  should be fixed to help improve UX of cluster upgrade.
* "[Call for action: Implementing Cluster Operator Condition Rules to Improve Upgrade UX|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/hih4j4Z7AAAJ]" is sent to the mailing list: [openshift-eng@redhat.com|mailto:openshift-eng@redhat.com] and [aos-devel@redhat.com|mailto:aos-devel@redhat.com].
* [Verification with Sippy of an OCP Bug on ClusterOperator's condition and Removal of its exception on the test|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/EQFrXocSBQAJ] is sent to the same mailing list as above.

h3. *New changed API rule*

[https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files]

* A component must not report Available=False or Degrade=True during the course of a normal upgrade.
* A version change is a config change. Operators must go Progressing=True when transitioning between versions.
* Operators should not report Progressing only because DaemonSets owned by them are adjusting to a new node from cluster scaleup or a node rebooting from cluster upgrade.
* A component in a cluster with less than 250 nodes must complete a version change within a limited period of time: 90 minutes for Machine Config Operator and 20 minutes for others.

|Operator compatibility|All core OpenShift operators|

h2. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

As a cluster-admin I want to get accurate information about the status of cluster operators and monitor the upgrade process without encountering false alarms.

* ClusterOperator must not report Degrade=True or Available=False during the course of a normal upgrade. OCP bugs haven been filed in this area [1].
* Operators MUST go progressing when transitioning between versions (We will need to decide how to enforce it. Ideas are [here|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJ1J9C3V4/p1758557182452289?thread_ts=1758555726.800399&cid=CJ1J9C3V4]). For now, this goal applies only to HA clusters.
* Operators MUST NOT re-enter progressing state when simply observing node lifecycle events such as scaleup/scaledown or reboots – primarily an issue for operators that observe DaemonSets continuously: bugs coming from OTA-1637.
* OCP bugs will be filed for the cluster operator that take too long to upgrade OTA-1626.

Eventually, with these changes we should have Accurate status reporting, clear and clean upgrade progress information, Stable Operator status

* The bugs in a single Jira query grouped by Component: [Bugs causing false alarms in ClusterOperator status during OpenShift upgrades|https://redhat.atlassian.net/issues/?filter=12483797]

* "[Call for action: Implementing Cluster Operator Condition Rules to Improve Upgrade UX|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/hih4j4Z7AAAJ]" is sent to the mailing list: [openshift-eng@redhat.com|mailto:openshift-eng@redhat.com] and [aos-devel@redhat.com|mailto:aos-devel@redhat.com].
* [Verification with Sippy of an OCP Bug on ClusterOperator's condition and Removal of its exception on the test|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/EQFrXocSBQAJ] is sent to the same mailing list as above.

h3. *New changed API rule*

[https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files]

* A component must not report Available=False or Degrade=True during the course of a normal upgrade.
* A version change is a config change. Operators must go Progressing=True when transitioning between versions.
* Operators should not report Progressing only because DaemonSets owned by them are adjusting to a new node from cluster scaleup or a node rebooting from cluster upgrade.
* A component in a cluster with less than 250 nodes must complete a version change within a limited period of time: 90 minutes for Machine Config Operator and 20 minutes for others.

h2. Feature Overview

The MCP Lifecycle Operator deploys tailored NetworkPolicy resources per MCPServer operand to protect from unintended data leaks and attacks. Each policy restricts ingress to the configured MCP port \(TCP\) while leaving egress unrestricted, and is garbage\-collected with the MCPServer.

h2. Goalsh1. Each MCPServer operand gets a dedicated NetworkPolicy restricting ingress traffic
h1. NetworkPolicies track port changes and are cleaned up on MCPServer deletion
h1. Implementation follows existing reconciler patterns in the MCP Lifecycle Operator

[https://github.com/kubernetes\-sigs/mcp\-lifecycle\-operator/pull/249|https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/mcp-lifecycle-operator/pull/249]

h2. Feature Overview

Enable OpenShift clusters on Google Cloud to use the native [GCP Karpenter Provider|https://github.com/cloudpilot-ai/karpenter-provider-gcp] for automatic node provisioning. Karpenter watches for unschedulable pods and directly provisions GCE VM instances with optimal machine type selection, spot/preemptible instance support, zone awareness, and automatic node consolidation.

*What this feature IS:* Deploy the GCP Karpenter provider alongside OpenShift on Google Cloud. Karpenter provisions GCE VMs directly via Google Compute Engine APIs based on workload demand — the same native-provider approach used for Azure (karpenter-provider-azure).

*What this feature is NOT:*

* Not a GKE Autopilot replacement — this runs on self-managed OpenShift
* Not the CAPI-based Karpenter provider (that uses karpenter-provider-cluster-api, a different architecture used for AWS)
* Not a GA replacement for Cluster Autoscaler — Dev Preview first

*Parent:* OCPSTRAT-3096 (OpenShift Karpenter Support on self-managed HCP and Standalone)

----

h2. Upstream Provider Analysis

*Repository:* [cloudpilot-ai/karpenter-provider-gcp|https://github.com/cloudpilot-ai/karpenter-provider-gcp]

||Dimension||Status||
|Stars|313|
|Latest release|v0.4.1 (2026-06-09)|
|Karpenter core|v1.13.0|
|License|Apache 2.0|
|Maturity|Alpha — active monthly releases|
|Maintained by|CloudPilot AI|

*CRD:* {{GCENodeClass}} (v1alpha1) — supports service accounts, disks, image selection (Ubuntu/COS), pod alias IP ranges, kubelet configuration, VM labels, and instance metadata.

*Comparison with other providers:*

||Dimension||GCP (cloudpilot-ai)||Azure (Microsoft)||AWS CAPI (k8s-sigs)||
|Version|v0.4.1|v1.10.2 (GA on AKS)|v0.2.0|
|Karpenter core|v1.13.0|v1.10.0|v1.4.0|
|Consolidation|Yes|Yes|No|
|Drift detection|Yes|Yes|No|
|Spot instances|Yes|Yes|Via CAPI|

----

h2. OpenShift Adaptation Required

||Gap||Severity||Notes||
|No RHCOS image family|Blocker|Only Ubuntu and ContainerOptimizedOS. Must add RHCOS support.|
|No MCS/ignition bootstrap|Blocker|GKE joins via kubelet config. OpenShift bootstraps via MCS ignition.|
|No CSR approval for node join|Blocker|OpenShift requires CSR approval — fundamental security model.|
|No CCO integration|Major|Uses GCP IAM directly. OpenShift requires Cloud Credential Operator.|
|No Machine API awareness|Major|Creates GCE VMs directly, bypassing Machine API.|
|No HTTP proxy support|Major|Required for enterprise OpenShift clusters.|
|No MCO integration|Major|Karpenter nodes cannot receive MCO day-2 config updates.|

CSR approval, MCO integration, and Machine API coordination are shared problems being solved for the AWS and Azure Karpenter efforts — solutions transfer directly.

----

h2. Phased Delivery

*Phase 1 — Dev Preview:*

# Contribute RHCOS image support to upstream GCP provider
# Implement ignition/MCS bootstrap for GCE VMs
# Integrate with CCO for GCP Workload Identity Federation
# Wire CSR approval for Karpenter-provisioned nodes
# TechPreview feature gate

*Phase 2 — Tech Preview:*

# MCO integration for day-2 configuration
# HTTP proxy support
# Machine API coordination for upgrade-safe node lifecycle
# E2E tests on GCP CI lane
# Documentation

*Phase 3 — GA:*

# Full MCO/MCS lifecycle management
# Consolidation validation on OpenShift
# Performance benchmarking vs Cluster Autoscaler on GCP
# Multi-arch support (x86 + ARM on GCP T2A)

----

h2. Goals

# *GCP parity for Karpenter* — OpenShift on GCP gets the same Karpenter-based node provisioning available on AWS (via CAPI) and Azure (via native provider). Currently gap #31 in the Karpenter feature gaps analysis.
# *Faster node provisioning* — Replace Cluster Autoscaler 3-4 min provisioning with Karpenter 45-60 second bin-packing.
# *Cost optimization* — Heterogeneous machine type selection and automatic consolidation reduce compute costs. Spot/preemptible support included.
# *Multi-cloud Karpenter story* — Same abstractions (NodePool, NodeClaim, GCENodeClass) regardless of cloud.

----

h2. Deployment Considerations

||Consideration||Value||
|Self-managed, managed, or both|Self-managed first|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|Yes — primary target|
|Hosted control planes|Future|
|Multi node, Compact, SNO|Multi-node only|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Connected first. Restricted requires HTTP proxy (Phase 2).|
|Architectures|x86_64 first. ARM (GCP T2A) in Phase 3.|
|Backport needed|No|

----

h2. Upstream Engagement

The GCP provider is maintained by CloudPilot AI (commercial entity), NOT under kubernetes-sigs. Recommended approach: contribute RHCOS/ignition support upstream, evaluate receptiveness. If upstream collaboration works, maintain it. Propose move to kubernetes-sigs via SIG-Autoscaling in parallel.

----

h2. References

* GCP Karpenter Provider: https://github.com/cloudpilot-ai/karpenter-provider-gcp
* AWS CAPI Karpenter Dev Preview: OCPSTRAT-3096
* Azure Native Karpenter: OCPSTRAT-3096
* Karpenter Feature Gaps Analysis: internal
* GKE Autopilot (competitive): uses Karpenter internally

items.fromString: This work item is related to CNV-66837

h3. Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)

There is currently no way to monitor multipath status via Prometheus on OpenShift nodes. Customers using Fibre Channel storage with multipath must manually SSH into nodes and run {{multipath -ll}} to detect path failures. This feature would expose multipath path status as Prometheus metrics, enabling automated alerting on path degradation or loss — correlated to the affected PVCs and workloads.

h3. Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)

* Cluster admins can monitor multipath path health from Prometheus-compatible dashboards without node-level access
* Alerts fire automatically when Fibre Channel paths degrade or are lost, distinguishing physical link loss from logical issues
* Alerts correlate to affected PVCs and the pods or VMs that consume them, so admins can immediately assess blast radius
* Consistent metrics format regardless of the underlying multipath configuration

h3. Use Cases

# *Switch port failure — cluster-level alert:* A Fibre Channel switch port fails, causing path degradation on multiple nodes simultaneously. A single cluster-level alert fires identifying all affected nodes, enabling the infrastructure team to correlate the failure to a single physical cause (switch port, cable, or HBA) rather than investigating each node independently.
# *Namespace-level workload impact notification:* When multipath degradation affects PVCs bound to workloads, a separate namespace-level alert fires for each namespace that has impacted pods or VMs. This allows namespace owners and application teams to be notified about storage risk to their own workloads without receiving cluster-wide noise.
# *Planned SAN maintenance validation:* Before and after SAN fabric maintenance, an admin checks multipath metrics to confirm all paths are healthy and no workload is running degraded.
# *Blast radius assessment during an outage:* A storage array controller fails. Multiple multipath devices across several nodes degrade simultaneously. The admin queries Prometheus to get a list of all affected VMs and PVCs without logging into each node.
# *Capacity planning and reliability trending:* Over time, repeated path flaps on specific HBAs or switch ports show up in metrics history, helping identify unreliable hardware before it causes an outage.
# *OCP-Virt live migration decisions:* A VM's underlying multipath device is degraded to a single path. The admin or an automated policy can decide to live-migrate the VM to a healthier node before the remaining path fails.

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)

* Per-multipath-device metrics are exposed to the in-cluster Prometheus (total paths, active paths, failed paths, path state)
* Metrics correlate multipath devices to PersistentVolumeClaims and their consuming Pods/VirtualMachines via labels
* A cluster-level PrometheusRule fires a single alert when multipath degradation affects multiple nodes (e.g. a shared switch port failure), grouping the affected nodes rather than alerting per-node
* A namespace-level PrometheusRule fires one alert per namespace that has workloads (Pods or VMs) consuming PVCs on degraded multipath devices
* Metrics cover dm-multipath devices served over Fibre Channel
* Works on baremetal and any platform where multipath + FC is configured

||*Deployment considerations*||*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*||
|Self-managed, managed, or both|Self-managed (baremetal primarily)|
|Classic (standalone cluster) / HCP / SNO|Classic and compact; HCP worker nodes|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Both|
|Architectures|x86_64, aarch64|
|Backport needed|No|
|UI need|Covered by OBSDA-956 (alert management UI)|

h3. Implementation Plan

A per-node metrics exporter discovers multipath devices, resolves them to PVs/PVCs via device-mapper and CSI volume mappings, and exposes the result as Prometheus metrics scraped via a ServiceMonitor.

h3. Out of Scope

* iSCSI multipath monitoring (may follow in a later phase)
* Storage performance metrics (IOPS, latency) — covered by CSI Volume Health ([https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3190|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3190|smart-link] that is yet to be implemented and adopted by all storage providers)
* Multipath configuration management
* Alert management UI (covered by OBSDA-956)

h3. Background

Customer on OCP 4.18 baremetal with Hosted Control Planes and OCP-Virt, using HPE CSI driver with Fibre Channel multipath. They need metrics to validate physical link loss vs logical loss. Today the only method is {{oc debug node}} + {{chroot /host}} + {{multipath -ll}}. See RFE-8653.

h3. Customer Considerations

Directly driven by customer request (RFE-8653). The customer's architecture makes multipath monitoring critical for operational visibility.

h3. Documentation Considerations

* KB or docs describing the new metrics, the cluster-level and namespace-level alerts, and how to build custom dashboards around them

h3. Interoperability Considerations

* Related to OCPSTRAT-3190 (CSI Volume Health) — complementary but distinct: Volume Health covers CSI-level events, this covers host-level multipath path status
* Existing epic CNV-66837 "Add storage connectivity and health alerts" is already in progress under RFE-8653, targeting CNV v5.0.0
* Alert UI surfaces via OBSDA-956
* Relevant to any FC storage vendor (HPE, NetApp, Pure, etc.)

h3. Use Cases

# *Switch port failure — cluster-level alert:* A Fibre Channel switch port fails, causing path degradation on multiple nodes simultaneously. A single cluster-level alert fires identifying all affected nodes, enabling the infrastructure team to correlate the failure to a single physical cause (switch port, cable, or HBA) rather than investigating each node independently.
# *Namespace-level workload impact notification:* When multipath degradation affects PVCs bound to workloads, a separate namespace-level alert fires for each namespace that has impacted pods or VMs. This allows namespace owners and application teams to be notified about storage risk to their own workloads without receiving cluster-wide noise.
# *Planned SAN maintenance validation:* Before and after SAN fabric maintenance, an admin checks multipath metrics to confirm all paths are healthy and no workload is running degraded.
# *Blast radius assessment during an outage:* A storage array controller fails. Multiple multipath devices across several nodes degrade simultaneously. The admin queries Prometheus to get a list of all affected VMs and PVCs without logging into each node.
# *Capacity planning and reliability trending:* Over time, repeated path flaps on specific HBAs or switch ports show up in metrics history, helping identify unreliable hardware before it causes an outage.
# *OCP-Virt live migration decisions:* A VM's underlying multipath device is degraded to a single path. The admin or an automated policy can decide to live-migrate the VM to a healthier node before the remaining path fails.

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)

* Per-multipath-device metrics are exposed to the in-cluster Prometheus (total paths, active paths, failed paths, path state)
* Metrics correlate multipath devices to PersistentVolumeClaims and their consuming Pods/VirtualMachines via labels
* A cluster-level PrometheusRule fires a single alert when multipath degradation affects multiple nodes (e.g. a shared switch port failure), grouping the affected nodes rather than alerting per-node
* A namespace-level PrometheusRule fires one alert per namespace that has workloads (Pods or VMs) consuming PVCs on degraded multipath devices
* Metrics cover dm-multipath devices served over Fibre Channel
* Works on baremetal and any platform where multipath + FC is configured

||*Deployment considerations*||*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*||
|Self-managed, managed, or both|Self-managed (baremetal primarily)|
|Classic (standalone cluster) / HCP / SNO|Classic and compact; HCP worker nodes|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Both|
|Architectures|x86_64, aarch64|
|Backport needed|No|
|UI need|Covered by OBSDA-956 (alert management UI)|

h3. Implementation Plan

A per-node metrics exporter discovers multipath devices, resolves them to PVs/PVCs via device-mapper and CSI volume mappings, and exposes the result as Prometheus metrics scraped via a ServiceMonitor.

h3. Out of Scope

* iSCSI multipath monitoring (may follow in a later phase)
* Storage performance metrics (IOPS, latency) — covered by CSI Volume Health ([https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3190|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3190|smart-link] that is yet to be implemented and adopted by all storage providers)
* Multipath configuration management
* Alert management UI (covered by OBSDA-956)

h3. Background

Customer on OCP 4.18 baremetal with Hosted Control Planes and OCP-Virt, using HPE CSI driver with Fibre Channel multipath. They need metrics to validate physical link loss vs logical loss. Today the only method is {{oc debug node}} + {{chroot /host}} + {{multipath -ll}}. See RFE-8653.

h3. Customer Considerations

Directly driven by customer request (RFE-8653). The customer's architecture makes multipath monitoring critical for operational visibility.

h3. Documentation Considerations

* KB or docs describing the new metrics, the cluster-level and namespace-level alerts, and how to build custom dashboards around them

h3. Interoperability Considerations

* Related to OCPSTRAT-3190 (CSI Volume Health) — complementary but distinct: Volume Health covers CSI-level events, this covers host-level multipath path status
* Existing epic CNV-66837 "Add storage connectivity and health alerts" is already in progress under RFE-8653, targeting CNV v5.0.0
* Alert UI surfaces via OBSDA-956
* Relevant to any FC storage vendor (HPE, NetApp, Pure, etc.)

h3. Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)

Decouple the hard dependency between the OCP-Virt operator and LVMS/LSO storage operators in both the Assisted Installer and the Agent-based Installer. Today, selecting the OCP-Virt operator forces LVMS as a required dependency (with an additional disk requirement). This change makes LVMS and LSO available as optional standalone operators, allowing customers to install OCP-Virt with their preferred storage solution (shared storage like ODF, or local storage via LVMS/LSO).

This proposal was presented and accepted by the CNV team (June 19, 2026).

h3. Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)

* A customer installing an OCP-Virt cluster can choose to install:
** *Without LVMS or LSO*, if shared storage is provided (e.g., ODF, external storage)
** *With LVMS or LSO*, when no shared storage is available
* LVMS and LSO remain available as standalone operators but are no longer bundled as a hard dependency of the OCP-Virt operator
* Consistent user experience across Assisted Installer and Agent-based Installer
* No additional disk requirement forced on customers who already have shared storage

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)

* Remove the hard dependency: OCP-Virt operator no longer requires LVMS or LSO as mandatory prerequisites
* LVMS and LSO are available as standalone optional operators during installation
* Assisted Installer node verification no longer requires 2 disks when OCP-Virt is selected without LVMS
* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt reflects the same decoupling logic
* Existing customers who want LVMS/LSO can still select them during installation

*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed. Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*

||*Deployment considerations*||*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*||
|Self-managed, managed, or both|Self-managed|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|Yes|
|Hosted control planes|N/A|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all|All|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Both|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_64 (primary)|
|Operator compatibility|OCP-Virt, LVMS, LSO|
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|No backport to 4.22|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|Assisted Installer UI, Agent Installer UI|
|Other (please specify)|N/A|

h3. Implementation Plan

Implementation in two phases via child epics:

# *MGMT epic (Assisted Installer team)* — Implement LVMS/LSO decoupling in Assisted Installer first
# *AGENT epic (ABI team)* — Port the same changes to Agent-based Installer for OCP-Virt 5.0

h3. Background

*Current state:*

* Assisted Installer: When a user selects the OCP-Virt operator, LVMS is required with an additional disk. The node verification procedure expects 2 disks when LVMS is selected.
* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt: Inherits Assisted Installer logic. Even when LVMS is not available in the GUI, the LVMS image is added to the ISO.
* The same dependency exists for deployments using LSO instead of LVMS. There was a discussion about unification (see [PR|https://github.com/openshift/assisted-service/pull/6517]) which was not implemented because of the additional disk requirement when LVMS is used.

*Field feedback:*

* Customers want a storage solution for demo/PoC without requiring an external storage device
* VM live migration requires shared storage (e.g., ODF), and forcing LVMS/LSO creates confusion about storage options
* The forced dependency adds unnecessary complexity for customers who already have enterprise shared storage

*Decision:*

The CNV team accepted this proposal for both LVMS and LSO (June 19, 2026).

h3. Out of Scope

* Shared storage solutions (ODF, external storage) — provided by the customer
* ISO customization for additional Day-2 operators (long-term strategy)
* Changes to the operator bundle content beyond LVMS/LSO decoupling

h3. Documentation Considerations

* Update Assisted Installer documentation to reflect LVMS/LSO as optional
* Update Agent-based Installer documentation for OCP-Virt installation without local storage
* Update OCP-Virt installation guides regarding storage options

h3. Interoperability Considerations

* This feature impacts the OCP-Virt operator bundle configuration in both Assisted Installer and Agent-based Installer
* Related to [OCPSTRAT-3001|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3001]: Agent Installer for OCP-Virt — Day-1 w/o an external registry

h3. Links

* [OCP-Virt operator/bundle and user experience alignment — Proposal presentation (June 19, 2026)|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1vHarOlsbZbjCNpWxAMcYZA6ZMc4Ew6fujFNRJbq51e8]

{color:#0747a6}TLDR: In OCP 5.0, we want to announce GA for:{color}

* {color:#0747a6}*Day-1 installer*{color}{color:#0747a6} with 13 pre-selected Day-2 operators for OpenShift Virtualization w/o an external registry{color}

{color:#0747a6}*Day-2 upgrade/update*{color}{color:#0747a6} with an external registry provided by a customer{color}

{color:#0747a6}Day-2 add a new node w/o an external registry was moved to Day-2 upgrade feature ({color}[{color:#0747a6}OCPSTRAT-2791{color}|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2791]{color:#0747a6}).{color}

 

*OCP feature name:* NoRegistryClusterInstall

 

The installation process for the OpenShift Virtualization Engine (OVE) has been identified as a critical area for improvement to address customer concerns regarding its complexity compared to competitors like VMware, Nutanix, and Proxmox. Customers often struggle with disconnected environments, operator configuration, and managing external dependencies, making the initial deployment challenging and time-consuming. 

To resolve these issues, the goal is to deliver a streamlined, opinionated installation workflow that leverages existing tools like the Agent-Based Installer, the Assisted Installer, and the OpenShift Appliance (all sharing the same underlying technology) while pre-configuring essential operators and minimizing dependencies, especially the need for an image registry before installation.

Additionally, the offered functionality has to cover Day-2 (an adding new nodes) in a disconnected and (external) registryless environment.

By focusing on enterprise customers, particularly VMware administrators working in isolated networks, this effort aims to provide a user-friendly, UI-based installation experience that simplifies cluster setup and ensures quick time-to-value.

h1. Objectives and Goals

h2. Primary Objectives

* Simplify the OpenShift Virtualization installation and Day-2 (upgrade and adding new nodes) processes to reduce complexity for enterprise customers coming from VMware vSphere.
** Day-2 upgrade without an external registry will be delivered separately. A customer can upgrade the cluster using InternalReleaseImage CR for switching to an external registry
* Enable installation and adding new nodes in disconnected environments with minimal prerequisites.
* Eliminate the dependency on a pre-existing image registry in disconnected installations and adding new nodes.
* Provide a user-friendly, UI-driven installation experience for users used to VMware vSphere.

h2. Goals

* Deliver an installation experience leveraging existing tools like the Agent-Based Installer, Assisted Installer, and OpenShift Appliance, i.e. the Assisted Service.
* Pre-configure essential operators for OVE and minimize external day 1 dependencies (see OCPSTRAT-1811 "Agent Installer interface to install Operators") 
* Ensure successful installation/adding new nodes in disconnected environments with standalone OpenShift, with minimal requirements and no pre-existing registry

h1. Personas

h2. Primary Audience 

VMware administrators transitioning to OpenShift Virtualization in isolated/disconnected environments.

h2. Pain Points

* Lack of UI-driven workflows; writing YAML files is a barrier for the target user (virtualization platforms admins)
* Complex setup requirements (e.g., image registries in disconnected environments).
* Difficulty in configuring network settings interactively.
* Lack of understanding when to use a specific installation method
* Hard time finding the relevant installation method (docs or at console.redhat.com)

h1. Technical Requirements

h2. Use case:

OpenShift installation//adding new nodes with WebUI in a disconnected environment without an external image registry (all necessary components (RHCOS, OpenShift, and selected Day-2 operators) are a part of the mounted ISO image) for all Openshift deployments deployments:

* Single Node OpenShift,
* 3-Node with additional worker nodes
* Standard OpenShift cluster with dedicated control plane nodes

Additionally, support for x86_64 architecture (Aarch64, S390 and IBM-Z can be delivered as separate features after GA).

2 use cases:

* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt for Day-1 and Day-2 (adding a new node)
* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt for Day-1 and traditional approach for Day-2 with an external registry provided by a customer

h2. Image Registry Simplification

* Eliminate the dependency on an existing external image registry for disconnected environments.
* Support a workflow similar to the OpenShift Appliance model, where users can deploy a cluster without external dependencies.

h2. Agent-Based Installer Enhancements

* Extend the existing UI to capture all essential data points (e.g., cluster details, network settings, storage configuration) without requiring YAML files.
* Install without a pre-existing registry in disconnected environment
* Install required operators for virtualization ([OpenShift Virtualization Reference Implementation Guide v1.0.2|https://access.redhat.com/sites/default/files/attachments/openshift_virtualization_reference_implementation_guide_v1.0.2_0.pdf])
* List of Operators:
** OpenShift Virtualization Operator
** Node Health Check (NHC) Operator
** Fence Agents Remediation (FAR) Operator
** Node Maintenance Operator (NMO)
** Loki
** OpenShift Logging Operator
** Cluster Observability Operator(COO)
** MetalLB
** Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV)
** Kube Descheduler Operator
** NUMA Resources Operator
** NMState Operator
** OADP

* Note: we need each operator owner to enable the operator to allow its installation via the installer. We won't block the release due to not having the full list of operators included and they'll be added as required and prioritized with each team.

h1. User experience requirements

The first area of focus is a disconnected environment. We target these environments with the [Agent-Based Installer|https://console.redhat.com/openshift/install/metal/agent-based]. 

The current [docs for installing on disconnected environment |https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.17/installing/installing_with_agent_based_installer/preparing-to-install-with-agent-based-installer.html]are very long and hard to follow.

h2. Generala

* Productization of [OCPSTRAT-1985|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-1985] TP features
** Assisted UI
** Appliance

* Build Release pipeline for generic ISO
* Build Release pipeline for “above-the-sea” UI
* Support for OLM operator

h2. Connected phase

* It will be a new option in the Assisted Installer wizard.
* Selecting the new option, a user will receive a simple wizard leading to a customized ISO download.
* ISO will be generated upfront for each Z-release with the latest version of Day-2 operators:
** Minimum x86_64 architecture

h2. Disconnected phase

* Installation:
** Deploy: SNO, 3-Node with additional workers, Standard Cluster with dedicated control plane nodes
*** Including 4th and 5th control plane node
** Possibility to select operators from the predefined list during the installation process

* Upgrade/update:
** Day-2 upgrade without an external registry will be delivered separately. A customer can upgrade the cluster using InternalReleaseImage CR for switching to an external registr

* Expand the cluster with new nodes (scale out and node failure scenarios)
** Scale out scenarios worker nodes for below deployments:
*** 3-Node with 0..n workers
*** Standard OpenShift cluster with dedicated control plane nodes
** Failure scenarios:
*** Worker node failure
*** Control Plane node failure (minimum - document the manual procedure)
** Adding new nodes without an external registry
* Security:
** Authorisation and authentication of Assisted Service on a rendezvous node
** Admin - AI-UI session protection (HTTPS, credentials to access UI) during a cluster installation

h1. Definition of done

* Functionality described above delivered, tested by QE, and documented.

h1. Open question

* Installation monitoring - Once the rendezvous node is rebooted., it may require several minutes between the rendezvous reboot and when the console is effectively available, and during this “blackout” period, the user will not have any way to detect/spot an eventual issue
* Disaster Recovery

h1. Out of scope

* Shared storage solution which should be provided by a customer

h1. Links:

* [Agent-Installer Installation UI for OpenShift Virtualization - update|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gPmoOYhCq6ZasXIPkdT_p4_ENEAtUjPcE57P3xrV1SE/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.d5othfg3kle8]
* [Simplified Disconnected Installation|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oDoGvJprWPXSOzk-pM10B6g2UVZcr6u4xPVqMtDqhig/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.yh2dlzhij6zu]
* This document written by Zane Bitter as the Staff Engineer of this area contains an interactive workflow proposal.

* [PRD Installation UX for OpenShift Virtualization |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1em9AHbAAMvhVYupYBoV7kGzcwLjvN10OKdM-MtuZ2D4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.rla2ip2ik78](and notes from regular meetings)

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

This feature delivers support for WireGuard as a secure overlay transport within OpenShift Networking, aligned with the General Availability (GA) of WireGuard in RHEL 10.4 (targeted), which is expected to coincide with the OpenShift 5.2 release.

WireGuard provides a modern, high-performance VPN protocol with a simplified cryptographic design and efficient kernel implementation. Supporting WireGuard in OpenShift enables customers to leverage an industry-standard encrypted transport for cluster networking while aligning with the capabilities provided by the underlying operating system.

As part of the RHEL implementation, downstream support is planned for the Rosenpass project (potentially with modifications to improve configuration and user experience) to enable post-quantum cryptography (PQC) for WireGuard key exchange. This capability should be incorporated into the OpenShift design where appropriate.

At the time of this feature, WireGuard remains non-FIPS compliant and therefore cannot be used in FIPS-enabled OpenShift deployments.

IPsec will remain a supported option for internode traffic encryption. 

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

* Deliver supported WireGuard integration for OpenShift Networking.
* Align OpenShift support with the GA availability of WireGuard in RHEL 10.4 (targeted).
* Provide a supported encrypted transport option for cluster networking.
* Enable use of the RHEL downstream implementation of Rosenpass to provide post-quantum cryptography (PQC) capabilities where supported.
* Deliver an operationally simple and maintainable solution that integrates naturally with existing OpenShift networking architecture.
* Clearly define supported deployment scenarios and operational limitations.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

*Functional Requirements*

* Support WireGuard as an encrypted networking transport within OpenShift Networking.
* Integrate with the GA implementation of WireGuard provided by RHEL.
* Support the downstream Rosenpass implementation provided by RHEL for post-quantum key exchange where applicable.
* Provide mechanisms for configuring and operating WireGuard through supported OpenShift networking interfaces.
* Support cluster installation, upgrades, and lifecycle management using WireGuard where supported.
* Detect and appropriately handle unsupported deployment scenarios, including FIPS-enabled environments.

*Non-Functional Requirements*

* Maintain networking performance comparable to existing encrypted transport mechanisms.
* Preserve reliability during cluster upgrades and node replacement.
* Minimize operational complexity for administrators.
* Provide sufficient observability for troubleshooting and operational support.
* Clearly document supported configurations and limitations.

 

*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both| |

h2. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary).*      

+*Phase-3 Feature is for incomplete epics of*+ +*OCPSTRAT-2979*+

This feature aims to improve the user experience for cluster upgrades by providing more accurate and reliable status information for Cluster Operators. 
To ensure that operators behave predictably during upgrades and other cluster lifecycle events, and thus reduce confusion about the upgrade process.
This will be achieved by enforcing new rules for operator behavior and tracking compliance to address common issues reported by customers.

A successful upgrade path for a given {{ClusterOperator}} should follow a specific pattern:

# Before Upgrade starts, Operators are in a healthy, stable state: {{Available=True}}, {{Progressing=False}}, {{Degraded=False}}.

# When Upgrade starts the operator should become {{Progressing=True}} as it works to apply the new version.
It should *not* become {{Degraded=True}} or {{Available=False}}.

# After Upgrade, the operator should return to a state of {{Progressing=False}}, with {{Available=True}} and {{Degraded=False}}.
