|[+OCPBUGS-20056+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-20056], [+OCPBUGS-23746+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-23746], [+OCPBUGS-38661+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38661], [+OCPBUGS-38662+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38662], [+OCPBUGS-38663+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38663], [+OCPBUGS-38678+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38678], [+OCPBUGS-62629+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62629], [+OCPBUGS-62633+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62633], [+OCPBUGS-63116+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-63116], [+OCPBUGS-65896+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65896], [+OCPBUGS-65984+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65984], [+OCPBUGS-66027+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66027], [+OCPBUGS-66213+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66213], [+OCPBUGS-86308+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-86308]|

h2. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

As a cluster-admin I want to get accurate information about the status of cluster operators and monitor the upgrade process without encountering false alarms.

* ClusterOperator must not report Degrade=True or Available=False during the course of a normal upgrade. OCP bugs haven been filed in this area [1].
* Operators MUST go progressing when transitioning between versions (We will need to decide how to enforce it. Ideas are [here|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJ1J9C3V4/p1758557182452289?thread_ts=1758555726.800399&cid=CJ1J9C3V4]). For now, this goal applies only to HA clusters.
* Operators MUST NOT re-enter progressing state when simply observing node lifecycle events such as scaleup/scaledown or reboots – primarily an issue for operators that observe DaemonSets continuously: bugs coming from OTA-1637.
* OCP bugs will be filed for the cluster operator that take too long to upgrade OTA-1626.

Eventually, with these changes we should have Accurate status reporting, clear and clean upgrade progress information, Stable Operator status

* The bugs in a single Jira query grouped by Component: [Bugs causing false alarms in ClusterOperator status during OpenShift upgrades|https://redhat.atlassian.net/issues/?filter=12483797]
* The bugs in JIRA Dashboard: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|smart-link]  should be fixed to help improve UX of cluster upgrade.
* "[Call for action: Implementing Cluster Operator Condition Rules to Improve Upgrade UX|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/hih4j4Z7AAAJ]" is sent to the mailing list: [openshift-eng@redhat.com|mailto:openshift-eng@redhat.com] and [aos-devel@redhat.com|mailto:aos-devel@redhat.com].
* [Verification with Sippy of an OCP Bug on ClusterOperator's condition and Removal of its exception on the test|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/EQFrXocSBQAJ] is sent to the same mailing list as above.

h3. *New changed API rule*

[https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files]

* A component must not report Available=False or Degrade=True during the course of a normal upgrade.
* A version change is a config change. Operators must go Progressing=True when transitioning between versions.
* Operators should not report Progressing only because DaemonSets owned by them are adjusting to a new node from cluster scaleup or a node rebooting from cluster upgrade.
* A component in a cluster with less than 250 nodes must complete a version change within a limited period of time: 90 minutes for Machine Config Operator and 20 minutes for others.

h2. Email sent on Thu, Oct 23, 2025, 3:44 PM

h2. Call for action: Implementing Cluster Operator Condition Rules to Improve Upgrade UX

aos

Follow-Up

Hi all,



We hear from customers that upgrading is hard, that they are not willing to upgrade OCP unless necessary. In a decentralized upgrade process, every cluster operator has a play in building a more pleasant, confident cluster administrator experience. We are improving the OpenShift upgrade experience by standardizing cluster operator behavior, and we call for your participation in [fixing the false alarms in Cluster Operator status|https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2484].

*Problem*

During a cluster upgrade, cluster operators may report status that confuses a cluster admin

* Cluster Operators report {{Degraded=True}} or {{Available=False}} in a routine transition, which should only be used to state an outage
* Cluster Operators unnecessarily report the {{Progressing=True}} state during node reboot or cluster scale-up. 

These behaviors reduce an administrator’s confidence in the upgrade monitoring process.

*Solution*

Our solution, detailed in [https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469|smart-link]  defines clear, expected operator behavior during an upgrade:

#  *Before Upgrade:* {{Available=True}}, {{Progressing=False}}, {{Degraded=False.}}
#  *During Upgrade:* The operator *MUST* become {{Progressing=True}} (since a version change is a configuration change). The operator *MUST NOT* become {{Degraded=True}} or {{Available=False}} in HA Control Planes *UNLESS* there’s a critical failure requiring admin action. SNO / Non HA Control Planes not currently a focus.
#  *After Upgrade:* Return to the healthy, stable state: {{Available=True}}, {{Progressing=False}}, {{Degraded=False}}.

We are also setting time limits for an operator to complete its rollout: a component in a cluster of less than 250 nodes must complete a version update within 20 minutes, the machine-config-operator must complete the version update within 90 minutes.

*Call for Action*

We need you to adhere to the API rules(implemented by [openshift/api#2469|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469]) in *4.22* by fixing the bugs reported to your component in [OCPSTRAT-2484|https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2484].

We call for your participation to adopt the new API rules(implemented by [openshift/api#2469|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469]) in 4.22. Your primary action is to deliver fixes for the relevant [OCP bugs|https://issues.redhat.com/secure/Dashboard.jspa?selectPageId=12390305] identified by [OCPSTRAT-2484|https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2484].

The OTA team will implement tests to detect operators that violate these new rules. 

*Starting in 4.23, these tests will be enforced and will block the release if violations are found.*

*Resources*

* [https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2484|https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2484]
* [https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469|smart-link] 
* [https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/pull/1842/files|https://github.com/openshift/enhancements/pull/1842/files|smart-link] 
* [https://issues.redhat.com/secure/Dashboard.jspa?selectPageId=12390305|https://issues.redhat.com/secure/Dashboard.jspa?selectPageId=12390305|smart-link]

h2. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary).*      

+*Phase-3 Feature is for incomplete epics of*+ +*OCPSTRAT-2979*+

This feature aims to improve the user experience for cluster upgrades by providing more accurate and reliable status information for Cluster Operators. 
To ensure that operators behave predictably during upgrades and other cluster lifecycle events, and thus reduce confusion about the upgrade process.
This will be achieved by enforcing new rules for operator behavior and tracking compliance to address common issues reported by customers.

A successful upgrade path for a given {{ClusterOperator}} should follow a specific pattern:

# Before Upgrade starts, Operators are in a healthy, stable state: {{Available=True}}, {{Progressing=False}}, {{Degraded=False}}.

# When Upgrade starts the operator should become {{Progressing=True}} as it works to apply the new version.
It should *not* become {{Degraded=True}} or {{Available=False}}.

# After Upgrade, the operator should return to a state of {{Progressing=False}}, with {{Available=True}} and {{Degraded=False}}.



h2. Phase-3 In-Scope Bug list (14 bugs to be completed)

|[+OCPBUGS-20056+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-20056], [+OCPBUGS-23746+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-23746], [+OCPBUGS-38661+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38661], [+OCPBUGS-38662+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38662], [+OCPBUGS-38663+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38663], [+OCPBUGS-38678+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-38678], [+OCPBUGS-62629+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62629], [+OCPBUGS-62633+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-62633], [+OCPBUGS-63116+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-63116], [+OCPBUGS-65896+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65896], [+OCPBUGS-65984+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-65984], [+OCPBUGS-66027+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66027], [+OCPBUGS-66213+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-66213], [+OCPBUGS-86308+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPBUGS-86308]|

h2. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

As a cluster-admin I want to get accurate information about the status of cluster operators and monitor the upgrade process without encountering false alarms.

* ClusterOperator must not report Degrade=True or Available=False during the course of a normal upgrade. OCP bugs haven been filed in this area [1].
* Operators MUST go progressing when transitioning between versions (We will need to decide how to enforce it. Ideas are [here|https://redhat-internal.slack.com/archives/CJ1J9C3V4/p1758557182452289?thread_ts=1758555726.800399&cid=CJ1J9C3V4]). For now, this goal applies only to HA clusters.
* Operators MUST NOT re-enter progressing state when simply observing node lifecycle events such as scaleup/scaledown or reboots – primarily an issue for operators that observe DaemonSets continuously: bugs coming from OTA-1637.
* OCP bugs will be filed for the cluster operator that take too long to upgrade OTA-1626.

Eventually, with these changes we should have Accurate status reporting, clear and clean upgrade progress information, Stable Operator status

* The bugs in a single Jira query grouped by Component: [Bugs causing false alarms in ClusterOperator status during OpenShift upgrades|https://redhat.atlassian.net/issues/?filter=12483797]
* The bugs in JIRA Dashboard: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|https://redhat.atlassian.net/jira/dashboards/22315|smart-link]  should be fixed to help improve UX of cluster upgrade.
* "[Call for action: Implementing Cluster Operator Condition Rules to Improve Upgrade UX|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/hih4j4Z7AAAJ]" is sent to the mailing list: [openshift-eng@redhat.com|mailto:openshift-eng@redhat.com] and [aos-devel@redhat.com|mailto:aos-devel@redhat.com].
* [Verification with Sippy of an OCP Bug on ClusterOperator's condition and Removal of its exception on the test|https://groups.google.com/a/redhat.com/g/openshift-eng/c/vJBcrtmh9x4/m/EQFrXocSBQAJ] is sent to the same mailing list as above.

h3. *New changed API rule*

[https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files|https://github.com/openshift/api/pull/2469/files]

* A component must not report Available=False or Degrade=True during the course of a normal upgrade.
* A version change is a config change. Operators must go Progressing=True when transitioning between versions.
* Operators should not report Progressing only because DaemonSets owned by them are adjusting to a new node from cluster scaleup or a node rebooting from cluster upgrade.
* A component in a cluster with less than 250 nodes must complete a version change within a limited period of time: 90 minutes for Machine Config Operator and 20 minutes for others.

h2. *Deployment considerations*{*}{{*}}

|Deployment considerations|List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)|
|Self-managed, managed, or both|Both|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|Applicable|
|Hosted control planes|Applicable|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all|All except upgrade on SNO about Available=False and Degraded=True|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Applicable|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|All|
|Operator compatibility|All core OpenShift operators|
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|TBD based on release schedule and customer demand.|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|The OpenShift Console  
Status command|
|Other (please specify)|N/A|

h2. *Documentation Considerations*

explain the new operator status behavior during upgrades. Degraded or Unavailable status during an upgrade is now a sign of a problem, not just a temporary state. mention the time limits for operator updates.

+*Phase-3 Feature is for incomplete epics of*+ +*OCPSTRAT-2979*+

This feature aims to improve the user experience for cluster upgrades by providing more accurate and reliable status information for Cluster Operators. 
To ensure that operators behave predictably during upgrades and other cluster lifecycle events, and thus reduce confusion about the upgrade process.
This will be achieved by enforcing new rules for operator behavior and tracking compliance to address common issues reported by customers.

h1. Core OpenShift Payload Categorization for Selective Mirroring

h3. Purpose

* This feature introduces a mechanism to categorize the core OpenShift release payload into features, providers, and platforms, enabling selective mirroring. This empowers disconnected/air-gapped customers to filter out irrelevant container images (according to their platform provider and selected product features), significantly reducing disconnected mirroring transfer volumes, air-gap transfer overhead, and on-disk registry storage size.
* Each image in the core payload gets a machine-readable label of one of two types: providers and capabilities. The core payload carries an additional metadata structure that maps these labels to human-readable titles and descriptions. The lack of a label denotes a mandatory image.
* Administrators can implement label-based selection configuration for tools like {{oc-mirror}} in order to download an optimized subset of the core platform. This leads to smaller transit payloads and on-disk/registry storage consumption, and fully supports cluster installation and upgrade operations, but is tailored to what the customer actually uses. 

h4. Functional Overview ("What" and "Why")

For enterprise customers operating OpenShift in disconnected (air-gapped) environments, mirroring the core platform payload with tools like {{oc-mirror}} requires transferring the entire set of release images for each OpenShift release, regardless of the platform provider the customer targets or the OCP capabilities they plan to use. Currently, a standard release payload includes over 190 images, specific cloud provider integrations (e.g., AWS, Azure, GCP), platform-specific drivers, and optional features that are often irrelevant to certain deployment types, such as a local, private bare-metal datacenter. This absence of filtering causes unnecessarily bloated transport footprints over removable storage devices and consumes valuable disk space on local enterprise container registries, as on average 40% of the images can be omitted for a given platform provider type (e.g. for AWS, about 15 out of 35 GiB can be omitted, see here for more scenarios ([https://dmesser.github.io/openshift-payload-analysis/|https://dmesser.github.io/openshift-payload-analysis/|smart-link] ). This issue is compounding for each additional OpenShift patch released that must be mirrored, as those typically do not deduplicate well (large Golang binary rebuilds).

This feature introduces a declarative payload categorization taxonomy for the core OpenShift release payload, conceptually similar to how OLM catalog content filtering is handled under [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HPSTRAT-133|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HPSTRAT-133|smart-link] but focused on the core platform payload. By classifying core release images by infrastructure providers, platforms, and features and OLM-managed operator content, {{oc-mirror}} can dynamically pull only the matching subset of images specified by the cluster administrator, and introduce large storage savings across the board.

h4. Scope Details

* *In scope:*
** *Payload Metadata Schema*: Definition and injection of classification tags within core OpenShift release payload manifests to map container images to specific platforms (e.g., {{baremetal}}, {{vsphere}}, {{aws}}, {{azure}}, {{gcp}}) or features.
** *Tooling Enhancement*: Updates to the {{oc-mirror}} utility to interpret the new payload categorization metadata tags. Update the {{oc-mirror}} UI to render a human-friendly selection of core payload provider and capability filters.
** *Configuration Extensions*: Enhancements to the {{ImageSetConfiguration}} API schema to accept label-based filtering rules for the core payload based on providers and capabilities.
** *Backward compatibility*: Label-processing logic within {{oc-mirror}} to ensure older release payloads are still mirrored as is. The lack of a label is interpreted as the image being mandatory.
* *Out of scope*:
** Introduction of new, optional capabilities in OpenShift.

h4. Example Results (Upon Completion)

* The customer can run this command: {{oc-mirror --config imageset-config.yaml}}, containing core payload filtering directives for a vSphere-based installation.
* The system does this now if I run this command: filters out any cloud-specific or bare-metal related image to a vSphere-specific payload subset + the mandatory core images.
* The customer can successfully install and upgrade a disconnected OpenShift cluster using only the targeted, low-footprint mirrored subset without pulling unneeded images, saving about 15 GB of transfer volume and disk/registry space per OpenShift patch release. 

*Related work:*

* [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1s6yErh0CsujIFVr-Vop-ZoICVR49sS4L3obxlLleljE|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1s6yErh0CsujIFVr-Vop-ZoICVR49sS4L3obxlLleljE]

h4. Acceptance Criteria / Definition of Done

# *Taxonomy Implementation*: Every container image within the core OpenShift release payload is accurately categorized and tracked via manifest metadata.
# *Backward compatibility:* By default, everything is mirrored. The absence of labels denotes that an image is mandatory and avoids hard error messages from {{oc-mirror}}.
# *Tooling Enforcement*: The {{oc-mirror}} tool correctly resolves core payload labels and selectively mirrors based on the {{ImageSetConfiguration}} block criteria. Either inclusion-based or exclusion-based filtering rules can be expressed.
# *Deployment Verification*: Selectively mirrored core payloads are validated to ensure successful clean cluster installations and updates across target configurations (e.g., bare-metal) in air-gapped staging environments.
# *Footprint Reduction Metrics*: On-disk registry storage size and data transfer volumes show reductions matching the efficiency expectations defined in our image size analysis matrices.
# *Documentation*: Clear user-facing documentation is delivered, detailing the updated {{ImageSetConfiguration}} syntax options and providing a comprehensive list of valid payload category tags and examples of typical configurations



*Open Questions:*

* What is the user experience today if a required payload image is absent during the installation or cluster upgrade?
* Is there any opportunity to provide early feedback to the user in the installation process if an image required for the installation or upgrade is not available in the disconnected registry?

* [https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1s6yErh0CsujIFVr-Vop-ZoICVR49sS4L3obxlLleljE|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1s6yErh0CsujIFVr-Vop-ZoICVR49sS4L3obxlLleljE]

h4. Acceptance Criteria / Definition of Done

# *Taxonomy Implementation*: Every container image within the core OpenShift release payload is accurately categorized and tracked via manifest metadata.
# *Backward compatibility:* By default, everything is mirrored. The absence of labels denotes that an image is mandatory and avoids hard error messages from {{oc-mirror}}.
# *Tooling Enforcement*: The {{oc-mirror}} tool correctly resolves core payload labels and selectively mirrors based on the {{ImageSetConfiguration}} block criteria. Either inclusion-based or exclusion-based filtering rules can be expressed.
# *Deployment Verification*: Selectively mirrored core payloads are validated to ensure successful clean cluster installations and updates across target configurations (e.g., bare-metal) in air-gapped staging environments.
# *Footprint Reduction Metrics*: On-disk registry storage size and data transfer volumes show reductions matching the efficiency expectations defined in our image size analysis matrices.
# *Documentation*: Clear user-facing documentation is delivered, detailing the updated {{ImageSetConfiguration}} syntax options and providing a comprehensive list of valid payload category tags and examples of typical configurations



*Open Questions:*

* What is the user experience today if a required payload image is absent during the installation or cluster upgrade?
* Is there any opportunity to provide early feedback to the user in the installation process if an image required for the installation or upgrade is not available in the disconnected registry?

h3. _Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)_

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Enable users to add OCI-compliant registries as Helm chart sources in the OpenShift Console, providing feature parity with traditional Helm chart repositories. 

This is the follow-on to [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2629|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2629|smart-link], which delivered direct OCI URL support for individual charts, this feature extends that to treat OCI registries as browsable, authenticated chart sources.

OCI registries are now the standard distribution mechanism for Helm charts (since Helm 3.8). While [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2629|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2629|smart-link]  enabled installing individual charts by OCI URL, users still cannot configure an OCI registry as a persistent chart source in the Console the way they can with traditional Helm repositories. This gap forces users to know exact chart OCI URLs rather than browsing available charts from a registry.

Additionally, many enterprise OCI registries require authentication, which must be supported.

* Originates from: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-7114|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-7114|smart-link] 
* Prior work: OCPSTRAT-2629 (OCI URL support — Closed/Done in 4.22) 
* Engineering epic: [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HELM-693|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/HELM-693|smart-link] 

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

_The observable functionality that the user now has as a result of receiving this feature. Include the anticipated primary user type/persona and which existing features, if any, will be expanded._ {color:#0747a6}_Complete during New status._{color}

* Platform engineers and developers can add an OCI registry as a Helm chart source in the Console, equivalent to adding a traditional Helm chart repository today.
* Users can browse and install Helm charts from configured OCI registries without needing to know exact OCI URLs.
* Users can provide authentication credentials (username/password) for private OCI registries.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

_A list of specific needs or objectives that a feature must deliver in order to be considered complete.  Be sure to include nonfunctional requirements such as security, reliability, performance, maintainability, scalability, usability, etc._  {color:#0747a6}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

* Able to add an OCI registry to the Console as a chart source, analogous to how Helm chart repositories are added today
* Able to authenticate to the registry using username and password credentials
* Charts from configured OCI registries appear in the Developer Catalog / Helm chart catalog
* Chart install, upgrade, and rollback workflows function identically whether the chart source is a traditional repository or an OCI registry

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Expose the upstream Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler {{--enforce-node-group-min-size}} flag through the OpenShift {{ClusterAutoscaler}} Custom Resource. When enabled, the Cluster Autoscaler proactively scales up any node group (MachineSet) that has fewer nodes than its configured minimum, even when there are no unschedulable pods. This ensures guaranteed minimum capacity for workload spikes without manual intervention.

*What this feature IS:* A new boolean field ({{enforceNodeGroupMinSize}}) on the {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CRD spec that passes the existing upstream {{--enforce-node-group-min-size}} flag to the Cluster Autoscaler binary.

*What this feature is NOT:*

* Not a new autoscaling algorithm — the upstream flag and behavior already exist and are GA since CA v1.26.0
* Not a change to MachineSet or MachineAutoscaler min/max semantics — those remain the source of truth for node group boundaries
* Not a replacement for capacity reservation or node pre-warming — this enforces minimums, not pre-provisioning

h3. *Upstream Analysis*

||Dimension||Status||
|*Upstream flag*|{{--enforce-node-group-min-size}}|
|*Introduced in*|Cluster Autoscaler v1.26.0|
|*Default*|{{false}} (disabled)|
|*Maturity*|GA — documented in upstream FAQ, no alpha/beta warnings|

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

# The {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CRD spec includes a new optional boolean field {{enforceNodeGroupMinSize}} (default: {{false}}).

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Expose the upstream Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler {{--max-pod-eviction-time}} flag as a configurable field in the OpenShift {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CRD. Today, the pod eviction retry timeout during scale-down is hardcoded at the upstream default of 2 minutes. Workloads with PodDisruptionBudgets (PDBs) and long startup/readiness probes can exceed this window, causing unnecessary scale-down failures. This feature lets administrators tune the eviction timeout to match their workload requirements



h3. Goals (aka. Expected User Outcomes)

*Primary persona:* OpenShift Cluster Administrator managing workloads with PodDisruptionBudgets.

# *Configurable eviction timeout:* Administrator can set {{spec.maxPodEvictionTime}} on the {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CR to a duration value (e.g., {{5m}}, {{10m}}), and the cluster-autoscaler-operator translates it to the {{--max-pod-eviction-time}} flag on the autoscaler deployment.
# *Upstream-default fallback:* When the field is omitted, the upstream default of {{2m}} applies. No behavioral change for clusters that do not set the field.
# *PDB-safe scale-down:* Workloads with PDBs and pods that have {{initialDelaySeconds > 120s}} (or long readiness probes) can be safely evicted during scale-down without hitting the eviction retry timeout, eliminating spurious scale-down failures.

*Expands:* The existing {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CRD configuration surface (alongside {{maxPodGracePeriod}}, {{scaleDown.*}}, etc.).



h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

# A new optional field {{maxPodEvictionTime}} (type: {{string}}, duration format e.g., {{5m}}, {{10m}}) is added to the {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CRD spec at the top level (alongside {{maxPodGracePeriod}}).
# When set, the cluster-autoscaler-operator passes {{--max-pod-eviction-time=<value>}} to the autoscaler deployment's container args.
# When omitted or empty, the upstream default ({{2m}}) applies — no flag is passed.
# CRD validation accepts valid Go duration strings and rejects invalid values.
# The field is upgrade/downgrade safe: older operators ignore the new field; removal on downgrade reverts to the 2m default.
# Unit tests in {{clusterautoscaler_test.go}} verify:
#* Field is translated to the correct flag
#* Omitted field does not produce the flag
#* Invalid durations are rejected
# E2E test verifies the autoscaler pod starts with the {{--max-pod-eviction-time}} flag when configured.

{color:#676767}*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*{color}

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both|both|

|Connected / Restricted Network|Connected|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_x64, ARM (aarch64)|
|Operator compatibility| |
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|No|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|No|

h3. *Use Cases (Optional):*

{color:#676767}_Include use case diagrams, main success scenarios, alternative flow scenarios._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

*UC1: PDB + Long Startup Probe (customer-reported scenario)*

Based on the real customer scenario from case 04472374:

* Customer runs a deployment ({{ignite}}) with 9 replicas and a PDB ({{maxUnavailable: 1}}, {{disruptionsAllowed: 1}}).
* Pods have {{initialDelaySeconds: 180}} on their readiness probe.
* Two pods co-locate on a node that the autoscaler identifies as unneeded during scale-down.
* The autoscaler can evict the first pod (PDB allows 1 disruption). But before evicting the second, the replacement pod for the first must pass its readiness probe — which takes up to 180 seconds.
* The 2-minute eviction retry window ({{--max-pod-eviction-time}} default) expires before the replacement pod is ready, the second eviction never succeeds, and the node is spared.
* With {{maxPodEvictionTime: 5m}}: the eviction retries for 5 minutes, the replacement pod starts in ~3m, PDB allows the second eviction, and scale-down completes.

Customer PDB configuration:

{noformat}apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: ignite
  namespace: nova-kontingent-prod
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ignite
status:
  currentHealthy: 9
  desiredHealthy: 8
  disruptionsAllowed: 1
  expectedPods: 9
{noformat}

*UC2: Default Behavior Unchanged*

* Administrator does not set {{maxPodEvictionTime}} on the ClusterAutoscaler CR.
* Autoscaler behavior is identical to today (2m default).

h3. *Background*

The upstream --max-pod-eviction-time flag was introduced in Cluster Autoscaler 1.25.0 via [kubernetes/autoscaler#4842|https://github.com/kubernetes/autoscaler/pull/4842], converting a previously hardcoded 2-minute constant into a configurable flag. The OpenShift fork already includes this flag via upstream rebase ([openshift/kubernetes-autoscaler#231|https://github.com/openshift/kubernetes-autoscaler/pull/231]), but the cluster-autoscaler-operator does not expose it in the ClusterAutoscaler CRD.

This is functionally distinct from maxPodGracePeriod (--max-graceful-termination-sec):

||*Flag*||*Default*||*Controls*||
|--max-pod-eviction-time|2m|How long CA retries the eviction API call if it keeps failing (e.g., PDB blocks it)|
|--max-graceful-termination-sec|600 (10m)|How long kubelet gives the pod to shut down gracefully after eviction is accepted|

Neither GKE nor AKS expose --max-pod-eviction-time. EKS users set it directly on self-managed autoscaler deployments. OpenShift providing a first-class CRD field is a differentiation point.

h3. Architecture Diagram

{noformat}apiVersion: autoscaling.openshift.io/v1
kind: ClusterAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  maxPodGracePeriod: 300
  maxPodEvictionTime: "5m"      # NEW
  maxNodeProvisionTime: "15m"
  scaleDown:
    enabled: true
    # ... etc ...{noformat}

{noformat}ClusterAutoscaler CR (user-facing)
  spec.maxPodEvictionTime: "5m"
         │
         ▼
cluster-autoscaler-operator
  AutoscalerArgs() reads field
  appends: --max-pod-eviction-time=5m
         │
         ▼
cluster-autoscaler Deployment (managed by operator)
  containers:
    args:
      - --max-pod-eviction-time=5m
         │
         ▼
cluster-autoscaler binary (upstream, already supports flag)
  config.MaxPodEvictionTime = 5m
         │
         ▼
Scale-down drain logic (core/scaledown/actuation/drain.go)
  retryUntil = time.Now().Add(5m)  // instead of default 2m
{noformat}



h3. *Customer Considerations*

{color:#676767}_Provide any additional customer-specific considerations that must be made when designing and delivering the Feature._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

* Add {{enforceNodeGroupMinSize}} to the ClusterAutoscaler configuration reference
* Add a "Maintaining minimum node group sizes" section explaining the behavior, use cases, and cost implications
* Note that {{minReplicas}} on the MachineAutoscaler defines the minimum that will be enforced

h3. Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)

The *Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Tech Preview 2 (TP2)* feature delivers the second interim milestone on the Red Hat OpenShift roadmap, building upon the initial TP1 milestone ({{OCPSTRAT-2465}}) and preparing the codebase for General Availability ({{OCPSTRAT-2739}}). Targeted for early August 2026 to directly align with the OpenShift 5.0 Early Access Program, this feature narrows its technical release scope to emphasize automated downstream verification testing, robust quality gating, and evaluation dashboards. It formalizes and validates the delivery chain where a cluster administrator installs the *MCP Server* via the *RHOAI 3.5 Operator*, which deploys the *MCP Lifecycle Operator* to manage the operational state of the server.

h3. Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)

* *As a Cluster Administrator / SRE*, I can reliably install the OCP *MCP Server* via *RHOAI 3.5 Operator* , which orchestrates the underlying *MCP Lifecycle Operator* .
* *As a QA / Platform Engineer*, I can access automated downstream verification results in a centralized dashboard to track {{mcpchecker}} metrics, trend analysis, and toolset execution health over time.
* *As an AI Application Developer*, I want OCP MCP server to be able to deploy in early bits of OCP 5

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):

h4. Functional Objectives:

* *Layered Operator Deployment:* Fully validate the structural deployment loop: *RHOAI 3.5 Operator -->MCP Lifecycle Operator --> MCP Server*.
* *Prow CI Automation:* Transition from manual QE verification ({{OCPMCP-73}}) to a fully automated downstream release pipeline in Prow, tracking auth/OAuth, gateway integrations, multicluster/ACM configurations, and client smoke tests.
* *Evaluation Dashboard:* Provision an evaluation dashboard parsing historical JSON test results to track capability regressions across differing LLM models and fast-moving toolsets.
* *Artifact Testing Isolation:* Ensure distinct, dedicated testing instances for server artifacts and gateway artifacts to guarantee clean environmental quality gating during Early Access evaluation.

h4. Nonfunctional Requirements:

* *Stability Gating:* Core reconciliation loops within the lifecycle controller must adhere to Kubernetes controller best practices to handle operational flux and architectural transitions gracefully.
* *Performance:* Downstream release testing automation must execute within standard OpenShift CI time-bounds without introducing flakiness into the release branch.
* *Agent Compatibility:* Expose dashboard output structures in a schema optimized for AI agents to programmatically query and diagnose failure vectors via dedicated tools.

h3. Deployment considerations



|*Scenario*|*Applicable Specific Needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|*Self-managed, managed, or both*|Both|
|*Classic (standalone cluster)*|Y|
|*Hosted control planes*|Y|
|*Multi node, Compact, or SNO*|All configurations supported|
|*Connected / Restricted Network*|All configurations supported|
|*Architectures*|x86_64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), IBM Z (s390x)|
|*Operator compatibility*|Y (Requires lockstep validation with the *RHOAI 3.5 Operator* lifecycle)|
|*Backport needed*|N/A|
|*UI need*|Web-based evaluation dashboard interface; evaluation of potential Sippy integration.|
|*Other*|External testing support from Yan Salani's team (e.g., Santosh) to be utilized for mid-August objectives.|



Use Cases (Optional):

* *Use Case 1 (Admin Onboarding):* An administrator triggers a standard RHOAI 3.5 installation. The platform automatically instantiates the MCP Lifecycle Operator, which smoothly establishes the default MCP Server instance without manual manifest construction.
* *Use Case 2 (Automated Regression Analysis):* A new patch is merged into the release branch. Prow runs the automated {{mcpchecker}} suite, writes out the JSON artifact, and updates the evaluation dashboard to instantly alert the team to a 5% drop in tool execution accuracy.

h3. Questions to Answer (Optional):

* What are the specific mapping requirements to integrate our custom evaluation metrics into Sippy dashboards rather than keeping them completely isolated?
* How will the RHOAI operator manage version drift between the platform lifecycle and individual MCP server images during the early preview phase?

h3. Out of Scope

* *MCP Specification Bump:* Adopting the {{2026-07-28}} specification is explicitly deferred out of the TP2 scope and shifted to the GA path ({{OCPSTRAT-2739}}).
* *In-Tree Documentation Hosting:* OpenShift local documentation will not house installation instructions for the Roy-installed operator vehicle; it will link out to external resources hosted in the Roy repository.

h3. Background

During the June 22, 2026 working session, the {{pod-yellow-octopus}} and OpenShift engineering teams adjusted milestones to manage transitions from component-based to module-based architectures. To defend the early August 2026 Early Access target, the general {{genie}} features and specification bumps were moved to the GA timeline. Technical priorities were condensed down to an automated verification ecosystem to stabilize the RHOAI-driven lifecycle delivery chain.

h3. Customer Considerations

* Moves customers beyond fragile custom scripts and Helm charts into a reliable, declarative, operator-led deployment path.
* Guarantees transparency of AI agent tool reliability through visible, automated evaluation metric trends before moving workloads to production.

h3. Documentation Considerations

* *Cross-Repo References:* OpenShift 5.0 early preview documentation will officially link to external documentation hosted in the Roy repository for the operator installation vehicle.
* *RHOAI Integration Guide:* Provide detailed step-by-step documentation for deploying via the RHOAI 3.5 operator framework, including configuring JSON retention policies for the evaluation dashboard.

h3. Interoperability Considerations

* Closely tied to *Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI)* platform onboarding milestones. Interoperability matrix testing must encompass standard, restricted, and multi-cluster ACM topologies to confirm the full stability of the automated test suite.





*By the time of TP2* 

There will be customers who will be on OCP 4.22 - > they should be able to install MCP server via helm 

For a handful of OCP 5 EAP customers, they will only be able install MCP server vai RHOAI 3.5

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*

_An elevator pitch (value statement) that describes the Feature in a clear, concise way. Complete during New status._

Deliver a *Tech Preview 1.z (TP-1.z)* release of the MCP server for Red Hat OpenShift in early August 2026 (to align in time for the OpenShift 5.0 Early Access Program). This is the *second interim milestone* in the MCP server for Red Hat OpenShift roadmap: it follows the initial Tech Preview delivered by [OCPSTRAT-2465|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2465] and precedes General Availability tracked in [OCPSTRAT-2739|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2739].

[TP-2] ships incremental improvements to the MCP server and its observability tooling — most notably updated *obs-mcp* tool metadata handling ([GIE-515|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/GIE-515], [rhobs/obs-mcp#110|https://github.com/rhobs/obs-mcp/pull/110]) — so that AI-assisted IDE and OpenShift Lightspeed (OLS) consumers can use observability tools with correct tool metadata and improved integration with the OpenShift Lightspeed console plugin. This enables the chat-to-Perses and user-initiated troubleshooting workflows targeting OpenShift 5.0.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

_The observable functionality that the user now has as a result of receiving this feature. Include the anticipated primary user type/persona and which existing features, if any, will be expanded. Complete during New status._

* *Developer persona* using generative-AI IDEs (e.g., Claude, VS Code, Cursor in agent mode) gains access to an updated MCP server build with corrected observability tool metadata, enabling reliable tool discovery and UI integration.
* *OpenShift Lightspeed (OLS) users* can interact with observability MCP tools (Prometheus, Thanos, Alertmanager, Tempo, Loki) without broken tool metadata that previously required consumers to read nested {{AdditionalFields}} keys.
* *Platform operators* receive a [TP-2] payload that validates incremental MCP server improvements before the GA milestone in [OCPSTRAT-2739].
* This feature *extends* the initial Tech Preview scope defined in [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2465|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2465|smart-link], and it does not replace or supersede the GA work tracked in [OCPSTRAT-2739].

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

_A list of specific needs or objectives that a feature must deliver in order to be considered complete. Be sure to include nonfunctional requirements such as security, reliability, performance, maintainability, scalability, usability, etc. Initial completion during Refinement status._

* *P0 — TP-2 release:** Ship an updated MCP server payload targeted for early August 2026.
* *P0 — obs-mcp tool metadata fix:* Incorporate the obs-mcp change that flattens {{AdditionalFields}} directly into tool {{Meta}} (fixes [GIE-515|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/GIE-515]; see [rhobs/obs-mcp#110|https://github.com/rhobs/obs-mcp/pull/110]), restoring compatibility with Lightspeed console plugin consumers that read {{toolMeta.olsUi}}.
* *P0 — Backward compatibility with TP-1:** [TP-2] must build on the [TP-1] foundation (OIDC/OAuth auth, read-only tools by default with opt-in write tools) delivered under [OCPSTRAT-2465] without regressions.
* *P1 — Documentation:* Customer-facing documentation updated via [OSDOCS-20234|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-20234] to reflect [TP-2] changes.
* *P1 — Evals / QE validation:* Eval / QE sign-off on [TP-2] payload including observability tool integration scenarios.

h3. Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)

The *Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server Tech Preview 2 (TP2)* feature delivers the second interim milestone on the Red Hat OpenShift roadmap, building upon the initial TP1 milestone ({{OCPSTRAT-2465}}) and preparing the codebase for General Availability ({{OCPSTRAT-2739}}). Targeted for early August 2026 to directly align with the OpenShift 5.0 Early Access Program, this feature narrows its technical release scope to emphasize automated downstream verification testing, robust quality gating, and evaluation dashboards. It formalizes and validates the delivery chain where a cluster administrator installs the *MCP Server* via the *RHOAI 3.5 Operator*, which deploys the *MCP Lifecycle Operator* to manage the operational state of the server.

h3. Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)

* *As a Cluster Administrator / SRE*, I can reliably install the OCP *MCP Server* via *RHOAI 3.5 Operator* , which orchestrates the underlying *MCP Lifecycle Operator* .
* *As a QA / Platform Engineer*, I can access automated downstream verification results in a centralized dashboard to track {{mcpchecker}} metrics, trend analysis, and toolset execution health over time.
* *As an AI Application Developer*, I want OCP MCP server to be able to deploy in early bits of OCP 5

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):

h4. Functional Objectives:

* *Layered Operator Deployment:* Fully validate the structural deployment loop: *RHOAI 3.5 Operator -->MCP Lifecycle Operator --> MCP Server*.
* *Prow CI Automation:* Transition from manual QE verification ({{OCPMCP-73}}) to a fully automated downstream release pipeline in Prow, tracking auth/OAuth, gateway integrations, multicluster/ACM configurations, and client smoke tests.
* *Evaluation Dashboard:* Provision an evaluation dashboard parsing historical JSON test results to track capability regressions across differing LLM models and fast-moving toolsets.
* *Artifact Testing Isolation:* Ensure distinct, dedicated testing instances for server artifacts and gateway artifacts to guarantee clean environmental quality gating during Early Access evaluation.

h4. Nonfunctional Requirements:

* *Stability Gating:* Core reconciliation loops within the lifecycle controller must adhere to Kubernetes controller best practices to handle operational flux and architectural transitions gracefully.
* *Performance:* Downstream release testing automation must execute within standard OpenShift CI time-bounds without introducing flakiness into the release branch.
* *Agent Compatibility:* Expose dashboard output structures in a schema optimized for AI agents to programmatically query and diagnose failure vectors via dedicated tools.

h3. Deployment considerations



|*Scenario*|*Applicable Specific Needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|*Self-managed, managed, or both*|Both|
|*Classic (standalone cluster)*|Y|
|*Hosted control planes*|Y|
|*Multi node, Compact, or SNO*|All configurations supported|
|*Connected / Restricted Network*|All configurations supported|
|*Architectures*|x86_64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), IBM Z (s390x)|
|*Operator compatibility*|Y (Requires lockstep validation with the *RHOAI 3.5 Operator* lifecycle)|
|*Backport needed*|N/A|
|*UI need*|Web-based evaluation dashboard interface; evaluation of potential Sippy integration.|
|*Other*|External testing support from Yan Salani's team (e.g., Santosh) to be utilized for mid-August objectives.|



Use Cases (Optional):

* *Use Case 1 (Admin Onboarding):* An administrator triggers a standard RHOAI 3.5 installation. The platform automatically instantiates the MCP Lifecycle Operator, which smoothly establishes the default MCP Server instance without manual manifest construction.
* *Use Case 2 (Automated Regression Analysis):* A new patch is merged into the release branch. Prow runs the automated {{mcpchecker}} suite, writes out the JSON artifact, and updates the evaluation dashboard to instantly alert the team to a 5% drop in tool execution accuracy.

h3. Questions to Answer (Optional):

* What are the specific mapping requirements to integrate our custom evaluation metrics into Sippy dashboards rather than keeping them completely isolated?
* How will the RHOAI operator manage version drift between the platform lifecycle and individual MCP server images during the early preview phase?

h3. Out of Scope

* *MCP Specification Bump:* Adopting the {{2026-07-28}} specification is explicitly deferred out of the TP2 scope and shifted to the GA path ({{OCPSTRAT-2739}}).
* *In-Tree Documentation Hosting:* OpenShift local documentation will not house installation instructions for the Roy-installed operator vehicle; it will link out to external resources hosted in the Roy repository.

h3. Background

During the June 22, 2026 working session, the {{pod-yellow-octopus}} and OpenShift engineering teams adjusted milestones to manage transitions from component-based to module-based architectures. To defend the early August 2026 Early Access target, the general {{genie}} features and specification bumps were moved to the GA timeline. Technical priorities were condensed down to an automated verification ecosystem to stabilize the RHOAI-driven lifecycle delivery chain.

h3. Customer Considerations

* Moves customers beyond fragile custom scripts and Helm charts into a reliable, declarative, operator-led deployment path.
* Guarantees transparency of AI agent tool reliability through visible, automated evaluation metric trends before moving workloads to production.

h3. Documentation Considerations

* *Cross-Repo References:* OpenShift 5.0 early preview documentation will officially link to external documentation hosted in the Roy repository for the operator installation vehicle.
* *RHOAI Integration Guide:* Provide detailed step-by-step documentation for deploying via the RHOAI 3.5 operator framework, including configuring JSON retention policies for the evaluation dashboard.

h3. Interoperability Considerations

* Closely tied to *Red Hat OpenShift AI (RHOAI)* platform onboarding milestones. Interoperability matrix testing must encompass standard, restricted, and multi-cluster ACM topologies to confirm the full stability of the automated test suite.

There will be customers who will be on OCP 4.22 - > they should be able to install MCP server via helm 

For a handful of OCP 5 EAP customers, they will only be able install MCP server vai RHOAI 3.5

The fix was merged in [rhobs/obs-mcp#110|https://github.com/rhobs/obs-mcp/pull/110] and needs to be consumed in a TP-2 MCP server release.

Design reference: [MCP server design doc|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1EJdKWjOB9K2SS86Fd6sIVX-9Gk-ey7k0E9Lu75o_w28/edit?tab=t.0]

h3. *Customer Considerations*

_Provide any additional customer-specific considerations that must be made when designing and delivering the Feature. Initial completion during Refinement status._
* TP-2 remains a **Tech Preview** release; customers should not expect production-grade support or stability guarantees.
* Customers on TP-1 should be able to upgrade to TP-2 with minimal disruption.
* Observability tool consumers (OLS, IDE agents) will see corrected metadata shape; any custom integrations that relied on the nested {{AdditionalFields}} wrapper will need to update.

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

_Provide information that needs to be considered and planned so that documentation will meet customer needs. If the feature extends existing functionality, provide a link to its current documentation. Initial completion during Refinement status._
* Documentation epic: [OSDOCS-20234|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OSDOCS-20234]
* Update TP release notes to position TP-2 as the interim step between TP-1 and GA.
* Document obs-mcp tool metadata changes and any new/changed tool behavior.

h3. *Interoperability Considerations*

_Which other projects, including ROSA/OSD/ARO, and versions in our portfolio does this feature impact? What interoperability test scenarios should be factored by the layered products? Initial completion during Refinement status._
* **obs-mcp** (rhobs/obs-mcp): primary upstream dependency for observability tools
* **OpenShift Lightspeed (OLS):** console plugin integration depends on correct tool metadata
* **Managed OpenShift (ROSA/OSD/ARO):** align with TP-1 deployment model; GA interoperability tracked under OCPSTRAT-2739

items.fromString:
h2. *Feature Overview*

As part of the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) 5.0 release, Red Hat is introducing  *Red Hat Core OS (RHCOS) 10* as the underlying operating system for the cluster nodes.

This feature specifically targets the *OpenShift deployments on Nutanix* to ensure it works with RHCOS 10, while maintaining full feature parity and backward compatibility with RHCOS 10. This enhancement ensures that customers can leverage new hardware capabilities supported by RHEL 10.

h2. *Goals*

The primary goal is to enable OpenShift on Nutanix to seamlessly handle the functionality regardless of whether the target OS is based on RHCOS 10.

*Primary Persona:* Cluster Administrator / Infrastructure Architect

*Expected Outcomes:*

* *Feature Parity:* All existing OpenShift on Nutanix capabilities function identically on RHCOS 10 as they do on RHCOS 9.

h2. *Requirements*

# Feature parity for OpenShift with RHCOS 9 and RHCOS 10 on Nutanix.

h2. *Use Cases*

h3. *Scenario 1: RHCOS 10 with OpenShift 5.0 Greenfield Installation*

As a Cluster Administrator,

I want to install a new OpenShift 5.0 cluster with RHCOS 10 on Nutanix as an infrastructure provider,

h3. *Scenario 2: Upgrade from 4.22 to 5.0 with RHCOS 9*

As an Cluster Architect,

I want to upgrade my OpenShift 4.22 cluster with RHCOS 9.on Nutanix as an infrastructure provider to the new version of OpneShift 5.0 with RHCOS 9,

h2. *Out of Scope*

*  

h2. *Links*

* *Master Ticket:* [OCPSTRAT-1150] - [Dual stream] Support two major versions of RHEL CoreOS in a single OCP release & cluster

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Enable GCP Workload Identity Federation (WIF) support in the OpenShift Custom Metrics Autoscaler (CMA) operator, allowing KEDA `TriggerAuthentication` resources to authenticate to Google Cloud APIs using short-lived, automatically-rotating federated tokens instead of long-lived service account key files. This eliminates the need to store static GCP credentials in Kubernetes Secrets, satisfying enterprise security mandates that prohibit long-lived credentials.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*



{color:#676767}*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*{color}

|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_x64, ARM (aarch64)|
|Operator compatibility| |
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|No|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|yes - console|
|Other (please specify)| |

<your text here>

 

h3. *Out of Scope*

{color:#676767}_High-level list of items that are out of scope._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

h3. *Background*   

Currently, to authenticate to GCP APIs, KEDA `TriggerAuthentication` resources reference Kubernetes Secrets containing GCP service account JSON key files. These long-lived credentials represent a significant security risk: if the Secret is compromised, the credentials are valid until manually revoked. Many enterprise customers — including Ford Motor Company — have security policies that explicitly prohibit the use of long-lived credential files.

GCP Workload Identity Federation (WIF) solves this by replacing static key files with short-lived tokens. The Kubernetes pod's projected service account token (a short-lived, automatically-rotated JWT) is presented to GCP's Security Token Service (STS). GCP verifies the token against the cluster's registered OIDC issuer and issues a short-lived GCP access token. This token is used for GCP API calls and expires automatically, eliminating the need for credential rotation workflows.

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Expose per-nodegroup (per-MachineSet) capacity metrics from the Cluster Autoscaler — including min, max, current, and target replica counts per nodegroup — so cluster administrators can build capacity dashboards that show when individual MachineSets approach their scaling ceiling.

Today, {{cluster_autoscaler_max_nodes_count}} returns a single aggregated total across all MachineSets. Customers managing multiple MachineSets (different instance types, AZs, workload pools) cannot determine which specific pool is nearing its limit. This forces them to either over-provision all pools or risk pod scheduling failures when a single pool is exhausted.

This feature contributes new per-nodegroup size metrics to upstream Kubernetes Cluster Autoscaler behind the existing {{--emit-per-nodegroup-metrics}} flag, then exposes an opt-in field on the OCP {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CR to enable them.



h3. Goals (aka. Expected User Outcomes)

* Query Prometheus for per-MachineSet capacity metrics (min, max, current, target replicas)
* Build Grafana dashboards showing capacity utilization per MachineSet
* Set alerting rules to fire when a specific MachineSet reaches 80% of its max, rather than monitoring the aggregate cluster total
* Make informed decisions about when to increase the max for a specific MachineSet before pod scheduling failures occur
* 

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

# *Upstream contribution:* New per-nodegroup size metrics MUST be added to {{kubernetes/autoscaler}} behind the existing {{--emit-per-nodegroup-metrics}} flag:
#* {{cluster_autoscaler_node_group_min_count{node_group="<id>"}}} — configured minimum replicas
#* {{cluster_autoscaler_node_group_max_count{node_group="<id>"}}} — configured maximum replicas
#* {{cluster_autoscaler_node_group_current_count{node_group="<id>"}}} — current replica count
#* {{cluster_autoscaler_node_group_target_count{node_group="<id>"}}} — target replica count (desired by autoscaler)
# *OCP operator field:* The {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CR MUST expose a new optional field {{spec.emitPerNodeGroupMetrics}} (default: {{false}}) that passes {{--emit-per-nodegroup-metrics}} to the autoscaler deployment.
# *Opt-in by default:* Per-nodegroup metrics MUST NOT be enabled by default due to cardinality/storage impact. The field defaults to {{false}}.
# *Cardinality validation:* Scale profiling MUST be performed to measure Prometheus storage impact at 10, 50, and 100 MachineSets before GA.
# *Backward compatibility:* Existing aggregate metrics ({{cluster_autoscaler_max_nodes_count}}, {{cluster_autoscaler_nodes_count}}) MUST continue to work unchanged.
# *ROSA/OSD compatibility:* The feature MUST work on ROSA and OSD clusters where the {{ClusterAutoscaler}} CR is managed by the service.

{color:#676767}*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*{color}

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both|both|
|Classic (standalone cluster)|yes|
|Hosted control planes|yes|
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all|MNO|
|Connected / Restricted Network|Connected|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_x64, ARM (aarch64)|
|Operator compatibility| |
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)|No|
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)|No|
|Other (please specify)|Upstream Kubernetes autoscaler contribution required|

h3. *Use Cases (Optional):*

{color:#676767}_Include use case diagrams, main success scenarios, alternative flow scenarios._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

*UC1: Capacity Dashboard per MachineSet* A ROSA customer runs 5 MachineSets (3 AZs × general-purpose, 1 GPU, 1 spot). They build a Grafana dashboard showing each pool's current/max ratio. When the GPU pool hits 80% of max, an alert fires and the team increases the max before scheduling failures occur.

*UC2: AZ Imbalance Detection* A customer notices pods pending in us-east-1a but not us-east-1b. Per-nodegroup metrics show the 1a MachineSet is at max (10/10) while 1b is at 3/10. They rebalance workloads or increase the 1a max.

*UC3: Cost Optimization* A customer uses spot and on-demand MachineSets. Per-nodegroup metrics show the spot pool is consistently at max while on-demand is underutilized. They increase spot max and decrease on-demand max to optimize costs.

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*

{color:#676767}_Include a list of refinement / architectural questions that may need to be answered before coding can begin._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

<your text here>

 

h3. *Out of Scope*

{color:#676767}_High-level list of items that are out of scope._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

h3. *Background*   

The Cluster Autoscaler (CAS) exposes Prometheus metrics for cluster-level capacity: total nodes, max nodes, pending pods, scale-up/scale-down decisions. These metrics are cluster-wide aggregates — they sum across all nodegroups (MachineSets).

For clusters with a single MachineSet, the aggregate is sufficient. But modern OCP/ROSA deployments commonly use 5-20+ MachineSets across multiple AZs, instance types, and workload categories. The aggregate obscures which specific pool is at capacity.

The upstream CAS already has a {{--emit-per-nodegroup-metrics}} flag, but it only covers scale-up/scale-down decision metrics — not the basic size/capacity metrics (min, max, current) that customers need for capacity dashboards.

*Karpenter gap:* Karpenter exposes {{karpenter_nodepool_usage}} and {{karpenter_nodepool_limit}} natively. No gap

* Performance advisory — storage impact guidance for large clusters (100+ MachineSets)

h3. *Feature Overview*

This feature extends the firmware update capabilities within the OpenShift Bare Metal deployment stack (leveraging Metal3) to encompass a complete set of server components. Currently, Metal3 supports updates for *BMC*, *BIOS*, and *NIC* firmware. This enhancement adds support for upgrading *Disk*, *RAID controllers*, *CPLD*, and *TPM* to provide a comprehensive, end-to-end Life-Cycle Management (LCM) solution for server hardware (Day-1 and Day-2).

h3. *Goals*

The observable functionality that the user gains is the ability to perform firmware upgrades on all critical server components using the existing Metal3 framework.

* *Primary User/Persona:* *Cluster Administrator*.
* *Extended Functionality:* Expand existing Metal3 firmware update functionality to include:
** *Disk*
** *RAID controllers*
** *Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD)*
** *Trusted Platform Module (TPM)*

* *Business Requirement:* Address the critical need for an end-to-end LCM solution for bare metal server hardware within OpenShift Container Platform (OCP).

h3. *Requirements*

h4. *Functional Requirements*

# The Metal3 framework must be able to detect, validate, and execute firmware updates for *Disk, RAID controllers, CPLD, and TPM* components on supported server hardware with Red Fish interface.
# Support levels will depend on the capabilities offered by each server vendor.
# The feature must support the following specific Hardware Bill of Materials (BoM) models with defined priority:

* 
** *Priority 1 (Prio 1):* Dell XR8620t, Dell XR8720t
** *Priority 2 (Prio 2):* HPe DL110 Gen 11, HPe DL110 Gen12

h4. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Reliability/Performance (KPIs):* Upgrade time must be measured. 
** Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for the upgrade time per hardware vendor must be defined and validated before the General Availability (GA) version of this feature.

* *Maintainability:* The implementation must integrate seamlessly with the existing Metal3 update workflows (which currently support BMC, BIOS, and NIC) to minimize maintenance overhead for the operator.
* *Security:* Ensure the firmware update process for the new components adheres to all OCP security standards, including image validation and secure communication paths.

h3. *Use Case*

As a *Cluster Administrator*, I want to *upgrade disk, RAID controllers, CPLD, and TPM firmware* on my bare metal infrastructure during the maintenance window so that I can *ensure the long-term stability and security* of my hardware components using the built-in Life-Cycle Management solution (Day-1 and Day-2).

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional)*

These questions should be addressed by the Bare Metal Team architect during the design phase.

* How will vendor-specific implementation details and potential limitations for updating Disk, RAID controllers, CPLD, and TPM be abstracted within the Metal3 framework?
* What changes, if any, are required for the Bare Metal Host (BMH) Custom Resource Definition (CRD) to accommodate these new components and track their firmware status?
* What are the specific failure and rollback mechanisms for updates to these critical components (Disk, RAID controllers, CPLD, and TPM)?
* What are the defined KPIs (metrics and targets) for "performant firmware upgrades" for the Dell (Prio 1) and HPE (Prio 2) BoM models?

These questions should be addressed by the Telco BU and Engineering team:

* KPIs (upgrade time per component per hardware vendor, upgrade success rate per component per hardware vendor). 

h3. *Out of Scope*

The following items are explicitly out of scope for the initial implementation:

* Support for server hardware without Red Fish interface.
* Support for components other than BMC, BIOS, NIC, Disk, RAID controllers, CPLD, and TPM.

h3. *Links*

* *Related JIRA RFE:* [RFE-8429] - Extend Metal3 F/W updates
* *Existing Functionality/Base Feature:* OCPSTRAT-1794 (Reference for existing firmware update functionality/persona).

items.fromString:
h2. *Feature Overview*

The Agent-based Installer (ABI) natively orchestrates headless, automated deployments in disconnected environments using declarative configurations. However, if validation errors occur mid-process (e.g., incorrect network parameters, mismatched MAC addresses, or invalid configuration settings), the installation loop halts, requiring manual script rewrites and media rebuilding.

To provide a resilient deployment experience, this feature extends the ABI automation loop by integrating a local Graphical User Interface (GUI) directly into the bootable asset. Under normal conditions, background scripts continue to drive the cluster installation completely automatically. If a pre-flight or runtime validation check fails, the installer activates an interactive fail-safe wizard by launching the embedded GUI natively from the cluster's rendezvous host. Users can then visually correct validation parameters, alter configuration settings in real time, and optionally export a corrected set of configuration manifests to optimize future automation passes.

*Goals*

* *Establish an Interactive Fail-Safe:* Integrate the web-based UI directly into the disconnected automation loop to allow rapid manual intervention during site provisioning failures.
* *Accelerate Failure Recovery Times:* Eliminate the need for infrastructure administrators to debug via blind text consoles or rebuild bootable ISO media when simple field configuration parameters are wrong.
* *Optimize Continuous Automation:* Enable field technicians to capture manual modifications applied inside the web interface and export a corrected configuration package.
* *Maintain Broad Topology Coverage:* Ensure complete graphical fail-safe parity across Single Node OpenShift (SNO), Two-Node OpenShift (TNx), 3-Node Standard, and Multi-Node OpenShift (MNO) traditional topologies.

h3. *Target Personas*

* *Cluster Administrator / Automation Engineer:* Implements automated deployment configurations but requires an interactive safety net to troubleshoot environmental variables on-site without resetting the deployment cycle.
* *Field / Site Operator:* Uses the on-site user interface to quickly rectify local validation issues (such as static IP assignment conflicts) without editing low-level code or YAML files.
* *Quality Engineering (QE) Engineer:* Validates that the state machine properly pauses execution upon validation failure, triggers the local graphical interface, and cleanly resumes the installation loop upon user confirmation.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Automated GUI Fallback:* The installer state machine must automatically start the local web console inside the release payload if background automation scripts encounter an unrecoverable pre-flight validation error.
* *Explicit GUI Trigger Flag:* The installer must support a dedicated runtime parameter or boot argument configuration to let users force-start the cluster installation inside interactive GUI mode from boot onwards, bypassing default headless execution.
* *Local Subnet UI Accessibility:* The GUI must be served directly from the bootstrap/rendezvous host and be fully accessible via a standard web browser over the local network subnet without requiring an external internet connection.
* *Mid-Process Configuration Alteration:* The interface must allow users to interactively update cluster names, hostnames, roles, network mappings (NMState), and network boundaries via the web form fields.
* *Declarative Parameter Export:* The web console must feature a dedicated action to let operators download the fully corrected install-config.yaml and agent-config.yaml payload files directly from the active session workspace.
* *Unified Architectural Compatibility:* The local graphical interface pattern must integrate cleanly with installations utilizing platform:baremetal and platform:none infrastructure definitions.

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Concurrency and State Conflict Mitigation:* The installer state machine must implement strict resource locks to guarantee that the background automation routines and interactive user inputs do not conflict during execution transitions.
* *Zero Host Overhead Dependency:* The embedded user interface engine must leverage pre-packaged web components already present within the standard core OCP release payload, requiring zero external package pulling at execution time.
* *Visual Status Transparency:* The local interface must provide clear, human-readable real-time logging, validation progress bars, and targeted error callouts to replace silent terminal loops.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Mid-Process Configuration Modification Workflow*

* *Scenario 1 (Dynamic Field Correction):* * *As a* Field Operator,
** *I want to* use a local web interface to fix a duplicate static IP allocation conflict discovered during an automated cluster installation,
** *so that I can* successfully resume the data center deployment without canceling the operation or manually rewriting configuration code blocks.
* *Scenario 2 (Capturing Site Adjustments for Future Scale-Out):* * *As an* Automation Engineer,
** *I want to* export the updated cluster definition files from the local interactive recovery console,

Will the interface require an explicit "Resume Installation" command confirmation, or will it re-evaluate system validations automatically in the background?

h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Operating System Package Modification:* Allowing users to alter baseline operating system software packages or add third-party drivers interactively through the graphical console windows (the GUI handles configuration parameters only).

h2. *Feature Overview*

In strict air-gapped or "dark site" environments, deploying clusters using the traditional Agent-based Installer (ABI) workflow is challenging because it natively extracts the baseline Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) image and expects to pull the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) release payload from an external or local registry.

To eliminate the requirement for a local registry mirror while maintaining automated provisioning, this feature updates the ABI execution path to directly consume and re-use a pre-bundled payload ISO (such as one generated by the [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  ISO Builder). Under this workflow, *the generation of a secondary, site-specific bootable ISO file is entirely bypassed*. Instead, the openshift-install binary acts as an orchestration engine within the customer's local automation toolchain. It mounts or reads the existing pre-bundled ISO directly to extract the core release payload, core operators, and base packages, combining them dynamically with local declarative YAML files (install-config.yaml and agent-config.yaml) to drive the installation loop.

!image-20260612-112902.png|width=736,alt="image-20260612-112902.png"!

h2. *Goals*

* *Eliminate Media Duplication:* Avoid the storage, time, and disk I/O overhead of writing out a new, multi-gigabyte site-specific bootable ISO for every distinct cluster profile.
* *Enable Direct Automation Re-use:* Empower customers to utilize the pre-bundled "golden image" ISO directly inside their datacenter orchestrators and automated provisioning tools.
* *Bypass Local Registry Requirements:* Perform programmatic installations without needing an external network or a local enterprise registry mirror by re-using the container images packed inside the original ISO.
* *Support Broad Topologies:* Maintain complete workflow compatibility across Single Node OpenShift (SNO), Two-Node OpenShift (TNx), 3-Node compact clusert, and Multi-Node OpenShift (MNO) traditional topologies.

h3. *Target Personas*

* *Cluster Administrator / Automation Engineer:* Integrates the openshift-install command into automated infrastructure-as-code configuration pipelines where a central payload ISO serves as the reusable source of truth.
* *Quality Engineering (QE) Engineer:* Validates that the orchestration loop successfully processes the embedded registry payload from the input ISO without requiring an active mirror endpoint.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Direct Base ISO Consumption:* The openshift-install utility must accept a custom runtime parameter (e.g., --base-iso) pointing to a pre-bundled payload ISO, treating it purely as an input read-only package repository.
* *Bypass Secondary ISO Output Generation:* The execution loop must bypass writing a new bootable ISO file to the local filesystem, streaming or referencing the deployment assets directly to the target environment orchestration layer instead.
* *Dynamic Configuration Merging:* The installer binary must read local initialization configurations (agent-config.yaml or install-config.yaml) at execution time and dynamically bind those properties with the container payload contained inside the pre-bundled base ISO.
* *Strict Release Version Guarding:* The installer must execute a pre-flight metadata check to verify that the semantic version of the local openshift-install binary perfectly matches the release image version encapsulated inside the target input ISO, aborting execution if a mismatch is detected to guarantee platform maintainability.
* *Bypass Image Extraction Loops:* The tool must skip standard RHCOS image downloading and payload extraction logic, reading the required host operating system files straight from the mounted base ISO workspace.

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Zero Host Container Engine Dependencies:* The extraction, mounting, or reading of the input base ISO by the openshift-install binary must execute cleanly without requiring localized container runtimes (such as Podman or Docker) or root-privileged loop-device mounting tools on the administrative workstation.
* *Persistent Internal Registry Linkage:* The automation orchestration path must ensure that the deployment configurations configure a persistent internal registry on the cluster's control plane nodes that survives structural machine reboots and datacenter power events.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Registry-Free Datacenter Automation Workflow*

* *Scenario 1 (Automated Multi-Cluster Deployment via Shared Media):*
** *As a* Cluster Administrator,
** *I want to* pass an existing pre-bundled payload ISO into the openshift-install process alongside discrete site configuration files within my datacenter provisioning engine, *so that I can* automatically deploy multiple independent air-gapped clusters without creating or storing unique, massive bootable ISO files for each individual site.
* *Scenario 2 (Zero-Registry Local Lab Verification):*
** *As a* QE Engineer,
** *I want to* run the automated ABI test suite by pointing the installer binary directly to a pre-validated laboratory payload ISO, *so that I can* verify cluster installation logic in a completely registry-free isolated network layout without provisioning an oc-mirror instance.

h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Bespoke ISO Modification:* Compiling, rebuilding, or adding new application layers or operator images to the physical base ISO structure during this execution step (payload additions must be handled upstream during the original ISO Builder phase).
* *Non-Agent Installation Paradigms:* Updating or modifying standard automated paths (such as Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure or User-Provisioned Infrastructure) that do not natively route through the core OpenShift Agent provisioning subsystem.

h2. *Links*

* *Target Disconnected Architecture Strategy Formulation:* [|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g208bc748bc9_0_0][+Unified Flow Strategic Alignment Presentation+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g208bc748bc9_0_0]
* *Agent-based Disconnected Installer Comprehensive Engineering Roadmap:* [|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38][+Detailed Strategic Roadmap Specification+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38]
