* *Bypass Local Registry Requirements:* Perform programmatic installations without needing an external network or a local enterprise registry mirror by re-using the container images packed inside the original ISO.
* *Support Broad Topologies:* Maintain complete workflow compatibility across Single Node OpenShift (SNO), Two-Node OpenShift (TNx), 3-Node compact cluster, and Multi-Node OpenShift (MNO) traditional HA topology.

h3. *Target Personas*

* *Cluster Administrator / Automation Engineer:* Integrates the openshift-install command into automated infrastructure-as-code configuration pipelines where a central payload ISO serves as the reusable source of truth.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Direct Base ISO Consumption:* The openshift-install utility must accept a custom runtime parameter (e.g., --base-iso) pointing to a pre-bundled payload ISO, treating it purely as an input read-only package repository.
* *Strict Release Version Guarding:* The installer must execute a pre-flight metadata check to verify that the semantic version of the local openshift-install binary perfectly matches the release image version encapsulated inside the target input ISO, aborting execution if a mismatch is detected to guarantee platform maintainability.
* *Bypass Image Extraction Loops:* The tool must skip standard RHCOS image downloading and payload extraction logic, reading the required host operating system files straight from the mounted base ISO workspace.

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Zero Host Container Engine Dependencies:* The extraction, mounting, or reading of the input base ISO by the openshift-install binary must execute cleanly without requiring localized container runtimes (such as Podman or Docker) or root-privileged loop-device mounting tools on the administrative workstation.
* *Operate offline:* Building of the agent ISO should be possible using only the base ISO, in a disconnected environment with no existing registry.
* *Persistent Internal Registry Linkage:* The automation orchestration path must ensure that the deployment configurations configure a persistent internal registry on the cluster's control plane nodes that survives structural machine reboots and datacenter power events.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Registry-Free Datacenter Automation Workflow*

* *Scenario 1 (Automated Multi-Cluster Deployment via Shared Media):*
** *As a* Cluster Administrator,
** *I want to* pass an existing pre-bundled payload ISO into the openshift-install process alongside discrete site configuration files within my datacenter provisioning engine, *so that I can* automatically deploy multiple independent air-gapped clusters without needing to individually configure them through the GUI.

h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Bespoke ISO Modification:* Compiling, rebuilding, or adding new application layers or operator images to the physical base ISO structure during this execution step (payload additions must be handled upstream during the original ISO Builder phase).
* *Non-Agent Installation Paradigms:* Updating or modifying standard automated paths (such as Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure or User-Provisioned Infrastructure) that do not natively route through the core OpenShift Agent provisioning subsystem.

* *Eliminate Media Duplication:* Avoid the storage, time, and disk I/O overhead of writing out a new, multi-gigabyte site-specific bootable ISO for every distinct cluster profile.
* *Enable Direct Automation Re-use:* Empower customers to utilize the pre-bundled "golden image" ISO directly inside their datacenter orchestrators and automated provisioning tools.
* *Bypass Local Registry Requirements:* Perform programmatic installations without needing an external network or a local enterprise registry mirror by re-using the container images packed inside the original ISO.

* *Cluster Administrator / Automation Engineer:* Integrates the openshift-install command into automated infrastructure-as-code configuration pipelines where a central payload ISO serves as the reusable source of truth.

* *Bypass Image Extraction Loops:* The tool must skip standard RHCOS image downloading and payload extraction logic, reading the required host operating system files straight from the mounted base ISO workspace.

h2. *Feature Overview*

OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) environments deployed at strict "dark sites" frequently lack access to both external Red Hat registries and local enterprise registry mirrors. To solve this operational bottleneck, this feature introduces a user-interface-driven (UI-driven) workflow on [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  within the Assisted Installer (AI) console.

Users can visually design their cluster architecture and select required Operator Lifecycle Manager (OLM) operators. Instead of a static ISO, the console generates a downloadable, self-contained *ISO Builder CLI* tool. This binary is dynamically injected with the "above-sea-level" configuration parameters selected in the UI. At runtime, it executes with zero required arguments on an administration workstation to download, cache, and pack all required assets directly into a fully bundled, standalone *Agent ISO*, alongside matching openshift-install and oc binaries.

!image-20260612-111852.png|width=884,alt="image-20260612-111852.png"!

h2. *Goals*

* *Consolidate Disconnected Workflows:* Unify the disparate features of the OpenShift Compliance Appliance, Agent-based Installer (ABI), and Assisted Installer into a single streamlined paradigm for platform:baremetal and platform:none.
* *Remove Local Registry Friction:* Eliminate the mandatory customer prerequisite to provision, configure, secure, and maintain a local registry mirror using the oc-mirror tool at the ultimate edge deployment site.
* *Abstract YAML Complexity:* Deliver a seamless interactive experience where a cluster design configuration can be compiled into a runtime binary without forcing an unskilled site operator to manually edit configuration manifests.
* *Expand Target Portfolio:* Natively support all standard OpenShift topologies, including Single Node OpenShift (SNO), Two-Node OpenShift (TNx), 3-Node Standard, and Multi-Node OpenShift (MNO) traditional configurations with dedicated control plane nodes.

h3. *Target Personas*

* *Cluster Administrator:* Leverages the centralized cloud UI to specify infrastructure profiles, select operators, download the builder binary, and specialize the installation media.
* *Quality Engineering (QE) Engineer:* Requires standard, repeatable, and automated mechanisms to validate that localized ISO bundles are production-ready inside verification laboratories.
* *Field / Site Operator (Limited Know-How):* Executes a single-step automated cluster installation (e.g., plugging in a specialized USB key and booting target hosts) without requiring deep knowledge of Red Hat ecosystem internals.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Dynamic Configuration Injection:* The image builder binary must be dynamically assembled at download time by the [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  SaaS platform to hardcode user configurations (e.g., pull secrets, SSH public keys, network configurations, and rendezvous IPs) directly into the executable.
* *Flexible Build Environments:* The ISO Builder tool must support execution in either:
** A connected management environment where it communicates directly with external Red Hat registries.
** A disconnected staging laboratory, provided the builder workstation has localized network connectivity to a pre-staged local registry repository mirror.
* *Zero-Argument Default Execution:* Running the generated CLI binary with no arguments must immediately trigger asset collection and build processes using the embedded configuration profiles.
* *CLI Parameter Overrides:* The binary must support command-line flags to ingest explicit container image pullspecs (pullspecs), allowing users to seed arbitrary workload images into the target image payload at build time.
* *Comprehensive Media Output:* The tool must produce a localized workspace containing:
** A fully tailored, single-bootable Agent ISO media bundle.
** A structurally bound, exact-version-matched openshift-install binary.
* *Targeted Day-2 Payload Generation:* For Day-2 maintenance operations (e.g., updating a standalone third-party operator or pushing application layer configurations), the builder must support a payload-stripped generation mode. This mode omits the multi-gigabyte core OCP release image and the Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) root filesystems, packaging only the minimal delta artifacts required to update the cluster's internal storage layer.
* *Supported Core Artifact Ingestion:* The builder must natively download, pull, structure, and bake the following components directly into the local output archive:
** Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) root file media images.
** OpenShift Container Platform base platform release layers.
** Selected first-party Red Hat Day-2 operators.
** Arbitrary third-party OLM operator dependency sets.
** Customer-defined application workload layers inclusive of localized custom objects (ConfigMaps, cluster customizations, logos, custom RBAC definitions, OpenShift Virtualization VM templates, VLAN/Network mappings, Persistent Volumes, and Secrets).

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Workstation OS Support:* The downloadable ISO Builder binary must natively compile and run cleanly across Linux and Windows operating system environments.
* *Control Plane Storage Persistence:* The internal container registry provisioned on the control plane nodes via this deployment loop must utilize strict underlying volume mapping to guarantee full data persistence. The registry must recover automatically with zero data corruption following cluster-wide power interruptions or structural node reboots.
* *Optional User-Defined Local Encryption:* The ISO Builder tool must provide post-download configuration capabilities that allow enterprise administrators to locally encrypt sensitive configuration blocks embedded within the binary prior to media compilation.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Day-1 Installation Flow*

* *Scenario 1 (Day-1 Deployment):* > *As a* Cluster Administrator,
** *I want to* select my cluster parameters and core operators inside the cloud console and download a pre-configured image builder tool,
** *so that I can* locally compile a single bootable Agent ISO that contains all platform payloads, eliminating the need to set up an enterprise registry mirror at my air-gapped data center site.
* *Scenario 2 (Day-1 Provisioning):* > *As a* Field Operator with limited infrastructure platform expertise,
** *I want to* insert a pre-compiled bootable USB flash drive into a bare-metal node server and turn it on,
** *so that I can* initiate a completely hands-off automated installation workflow that provisions an operational cluster without fetching files from external network connections.

h3. *Day-2 Maintenance Flow*

* *Scenario 3 (Day-2 Single Component Update):* > *As a* Day-2 Infrastructure Engineer,
** *I want to* use the configuration builder to create a lightweight, payload-stripped patch ISO containing only an updated version of a specific third-party operator,
** *so that I can* update our air-gapped environment's persistent internal registry quickly without transferring large operating system files across our strict security boundary.

h2. *Open Questions to Answer*

* *Plugin Architecture:* How will the [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  Assisted UI elegantly show and allow the visual selection of third-party operators that lack an official upstream Assisted Installer UI plugin service?

h2. *Feature Overview*

In strict air-gapped or "dark site" environments, deploying clusters using the traditional Agent-based Installer (ABI) workflow is challenging because it natively extracts the baseline Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) image and expects to pull the OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) release payload from an external or local registry.

To eliminate the requirement for a local registry mirror while maintaining automated provisioning, this feature updates the ABI execution path to directly consume and re-use a pre-bundled payload ISO (such as one generated by the [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  ISO Builder). Under this workflow, *the generation of a secondary, site-specific bootable ISO file is entirely bypassed*. Instead, the openshift-install binary acts as an orchestration engine within the customer's local automation toolchain. It mounts or reads the existing pre-bundled ISO directly to extract the core release payload, core operators, and base packages, combining them dynamically with local declarative YAML files (install-config.yaml and agent-config.yaml) to drive the installation loop.

!image-20260612-112754.png|width=905,alt="image-20260612-112754.png"!

h2. *Goals*

* *Eliminate Media Duplication:* Avoid the storage, time, and disk I/O overhead of writing out a new, multi-gigabyte site-specific bootable ISO for every distinct cluster profile.
* *Enable Direct Automation Re-use:* Empower customers to utilize the pre-bundled "golden image" ISO directly inside their datacenter orchestrators and automated provisioning tools.
* *Bypass Local Registry Requirements:* Perform programmatic installations without needing an external network or a local enterprise registry mirror by re-using the container images packed inside the original ISO.
* *Support Broad Topologies:* Maintain complete workflow compatibility across Single Node OpenShift (SNO), Two-Node OpenShift (TNx), 3-Node compact clusert, and Multi-Node OpenShift (MNO) traditional topologies.

h3. *Target Personas*

* *Cluster Administrator / Automation Engineer:* Integrates the openshift-install command into automated infrastructure-as-code configuration pipelines where a central payload ISO serves as the reusable source of truth.
* *Quality Engineering (QE) Engineer:* Validates that the orchestration loop successfully processes the embedded registry payload from the input ISO without requiring an active mirror endpoint.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Direct Base ISO Consumption:* The openshift-install utility must accept a custom runtime parameter (e.g., --base-iso) pointing to a pre-bundled payload ISO, treating it purely as an input read-only package repository.
* *Bypass Secondary ISO Output Generation:* The execution loop must bypass writing a new bootable ISO file to the local filesystem, streaming or referencing the deployment assets directly to the target environment orchestration layer instead.
* *Dynamic Configuration Merging:* The installer binary must read local initialization configurations (agent-config.yaml or install-config.yaml) at execution time and dynamically bind those properties with the container payload contained inside the pre-bundled base ISO.
* *Strict Release Version Guarding:* The installer must execute a pre-flight metadata check to verify that the semantic version of the local openshift-install binary perfectly matches the release image version encapsulated inside the target input ISO, aborting execution if a mismatch is detected to guarantee platform maintainability.
* *Bypass Image Extraction Loops:* The tool must skip standard RHCOS image downloading and payload extraction logic, reading the required host operating system files straight from the mounted base ISO workspace.

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Zero Host Container Engine Dependencies:* The extraction, mounting, or reading of the input base ISO by the openshift-install binary must execute cleanly without requiring localized container runtimes (such as Podman or Docker) or root-privileged loop-device mounting tools on the administrative workstation.
* *Persistent Internal Registry Linkage:* The automation orchestration path must ensure that the deployment configurations configure a persistent internal registry on the cluster's control plane nodes that survives structural machine reboots and datacenter power events.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Registry-Free Datacenter Automation Workflow*

* *Scenario 1 (Automated Multi-Cluster Deployment via Shared Media):*
** *As a* Cluster Administrator,
** *I want to* pass an existing pre-bundled payload ISO into the openshift-install process alongside discrete site configuration files within my datacenter provisioning engine, *so that I can* automatically deploy multiple independent air-gapped clusters without creating or storing unique, massive bootable ISO files for each individual site.
* *Scenario 2 (Zero-Registry Local Lab Verification):*
** *As a* QE Engineer,
** *I want to* run the automated ABI test suite by pointing the installer binary directly to a pre-validated laboratory payload ISO, *so that I can* verify cluster installation logic in a completely registry-free isolated network layout without provisioning an oc-mirror instance.

h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Bespoke ISO Modification:* Compiling, rebuilding, or adding new application layers or operator images to the physical base ISO structure during this execution step (payload additions must be handled upstream during the original ISO Builder phase).
* *Non-Agent Installation Paradigms:* Updating or modifying standard automated paths (such as Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure or User-Provisioned Infrastructure) that do not natively route through the core OpenShift Agent provisioning subsystem.

h2. *Links*

* *Target Disconnected Architecture Strategy Formulation:* [|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g208bc748bc9_0_0][+Unified Flow Strategic Alignment Presentation+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g208bc748bc9_0_0]
* *Agent-based Disconnected Installer Comprehensive Engineering Roadmap:* [|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38][+Detailed Strategic Roadmap Specification+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38]

** A structurally bound, exact-version-matched openshift-install binary.
* *Targeted Day-2 Payload Generation:* For Day-2 maintenance operations (e.g., updating a standalone third-party operator or pushing application layer configurations), the builder must support a payload-stripped generation mode. This mode omits the multi-gigabyte core OCP release image and the Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) root filesystems, packaging only the minimal delta artifacts required to update the cluster's internal storage layer.
* *Supported Core Artifact Ingestion:* The builder must natively download, pull, structure, and bake the following components directly into the local output archive:
** Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) root file media images.
** OpenShift Container Platform base platform release layers.
** Selected first-party Red Hat Day-2 operators.
** Arbitrary third-party OLM operator dependency sets.
** Customer-defined application workload layers inclusive of localized custom objects (ConfigMaps, cluster customizations, logos, custom RBAC definitions, OpenShift Virtualization VM templates, VLAN/Network mappings, Persistent Volumes, and Secrets).

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Workstation OS Support:* The downloadable ISO Builder binary must natively compile and run cleanly across Linux and Windows operating system environments.
* *Control Plane Storage Persistence:* The internal container registry provisioned on the control plane nodes via this deployment loop must utilize strict underlying volume mapping to guarantee full data persistence. The registry must recover automatically with zero data corruption following cluster-wide power interruptions or structural node reboots.
* *Optional User-Defined Local Encryption:* The ISO Builder tool must provide post-download configuration capabilities that allow enterprise administrators to locally encrypt sensitive configuration blocks embedded within the binary prior to media compilation.

h2. *Use Cases & User Scenarios*

h3. *Day-1 Installation Flow*

* *Scenario 1 (Day-1 Deployment):* > *As a* Cluster Administrator,
** *I want to* select my cluster parameters and core operators inside the cloud console and download a pre-configured image builder tool,
** *so that I can* locally compile a single bootable Agent ISO that contains all platform payloads, eliminating the need to set up an enterprise registry mirror at my air-gapped data center site.
* *Scenario 2 (Day-1 Provisioning):* > *As a* Field Operator with limited infrastructure platform expertise,
** *I want to* insert a pre-compiled bootable USB flash drive into a bare-metal node server and turn it on,
** *so that I can* initiate a completely hands-off automated installation workflow that provisions an operational cluster without fetching files from external network connections.

h3. *Day-2 Maintenance Flow*

* *Scenario 3 (Day-2 Single Component Update):* > *As a* Day-2 Infrastructure Engineer,
** *I want to* use the configuration builder to create a lightweight, payload-stripped patch ISO containing only an updated version of a specific third-party operator,
** *so that I can* update our air-gapped environment's persistent internal registry quickly without transferring large operating system files across our strict security boundary.

h2. *Open Questions to Answer*

* *Plugin Architecture:* How will the [http://console.redhat.com|http://console.redhat.com|smart-link]  Assisted UI elegantly show and allow the visual selection of third-party operators that lack an official upstream Assisted Installer UI plugin service?
* *Validation & Status Indicators:* What reporting indicators will be exposed to the local terminal environment while the standalone binary downloads and structures massive image sets to ensure clarity regarding process progression?
* *Partial upgrade*: How can a user create an ISO for Day-2 (upgrade) only which will contain selected images (e.g., one Day-2 operator) to update the Internal Registry?

h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Hyperscaler Platforms:* Native integration or targeted optimization paths for automated cloud provider platforms (e.g., Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform).
* *Integrated Virtualized Infrastructure Control Planes:* Out-of-the-box automated target integrations with standard on-premise hypervisor infrastructure layers (e.g., VMware vSphere or Nutanix platform APIs) for this initial phase.
* *Shared Cluster Storage Provisioning:* The validation, architecture, and manual configuration loops required to support external cluster storage systems remain the sole responsibility of the customer.

h2. *Links*

* *Core Disconnected Installer Strategy Presentation:* [|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g3dda7d6adef_0_62][+Strategy Deck Link+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g3dda7d6adef_0_62]
* *Detailed Strategy & Engineering Baseline Specification Document:* [|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38][+Detailed Strategic Specification Document+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/13ePVuYzKgR8ozp0KWaQm56CupgEBLeM8gS_ODerAn9g/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.z04s4pfeic38]
* *Agent Installer for OpenShift Virtualization Development Timeline Reference:* [|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g3d056cd6e39_0_2744][+Roadmap Reference Link+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1S0ArVL1rZhfhlwQRvE5NeBNXbJk2DB-0AOJhf_k9nwc/edit?slide=id.g3d056cd6e39_0_2744]

{color:#0747a6}TLDR: In OCP 5.0, we want to announce GA for:{color}

* {color:#0747a6}*Day-1 installer*{color}{color:#0747a6} with 13 pre-selected Day-2 operators for OpenShift Virtualization w/o an external registry{color}

{color:#0747a6}*Day-2 upgrade/update*{color}{color:#0747a6} with an external registry provided by a customer{color}

{color:#0747a6}Day-2 add a new node w/o an external registry was moved to Day-2 upgrade feature ({color}[{color:#0747a6}OCPSTRAT-2791{color}|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2791]{color:#0747a6}).{color}

 

*OCP feature name:* NoRegistryClusterInstall

 

The installation process for the OpenShift Virtualization Engine (OVE) has been identified as a critical area for improvement to address customer concerns regarding its complexity compared to competitors like VMware, Nutanix, and Proxmox. Customers often struggle with disconnected environments, operator configuration, and managing external dependencies, making the initial deployment challenging and time-consuming. 

To resolve these issues, the goal is to deliver a streamlined, opinionated installation workflow that leverages existing tools like the Agent-Based Installer, the Assisted Installer, and the OpenShift Appliance (all sharing the same underlying technology) while pre-configuring essential operators and minimizing dependencies, especially the need for an image registry before installation.

Additionally, the offered functionality has to cover Day-2 (an adding new nodes) in a disconnected and (external) registryless environment.

By focusing on enterprise customers, particularly VMware administrators working in isolated networks, this effort aims to provide a user-friendly, UI-based installation experience that simplifies cluster setup and ensures quick time-to-value.

h1. Objectives and Goals

h2. Primary Objectives

* Simplify the OpenShift Virtualization installation and Day-2 (upgrade and adding new nodes) processes to reduce complexity for enterprise customers coming from VMware vSphere.
** Day-2 upgrade without an external registry will be delivered separately. A customer can upgrade the cluster using InternalReleaseImage CR for switching to an external registry
* Enable installation and adding new nodes in disconnected environments with minimal prerequisites.
* Eliminate the dependency on a pre-existing image registry in disconnected installations and adding new nodes.
* Provide a user-friendly, UI-driven installation experience for users used to VMware vSphere.

h2. Goals

* Deliver an installation experience leveraging existing tools like the Agent-Based Installer, Assisted Installer, and OpenShift Appliance, i.e. the Assisted Service.
* Pre-configure essential operators for OVE and minimize external day 1 dependencies (see OCPSTRAT-1811 "Agent Installer interface to install Operators") 
* Ensure successful installation/adding new nodes in disconnected environments with standalone OpenShift, with minimal requirements and no pre-existing registry

h1. Personas

h2. Primary Audience 

VMware administrators transitioning to OpenShift Virtualization in isolated/disconnected environments.

h2. Pain Points

* Lack of UI-driven workflows; writing YAML files is a barrier for the target user (virtualization platforms admins)
* Complex setup requirements (e.g., image registries in disconnected environments).
* Difficulty in configuring network settings interactively.
* Lack of understanding when to use a specific installation method
* Hard time finding the relevant installation method (docs or at console.redhat.com)

h1. Technical Requirements

h2. Use case:

OpenShift installation//adding new nodes with WebUI in a disconnected environment without an external image registry (all necessary components (RHCOS, OpenShift, and selected Day-2 operators) are a part of the mounted ISO image) for all Openshift deployments deployments:

* Single Node OpenShift,
* 3-Node with additional worker nodes
* Standard OpenShift cluster with dedicated control plane nodes

Additionally, support for x86_64 architecture (Aarch64, S390 and IBM-Z can be delivered as separate features after GA).

2 use cases:

* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt for Day-1 and Day-2 (adding a new node)
* Agent Installer for OCP-Virt for Day-1 and traditional approach for Day-2 with an external registry provided by a customer

h2. Image Registry Simplification

* Eliminate the dependency on an existing external image registry for disconnected environments.
* Support a workflow similar to the OpenShift Appliance model, where users can deploy a cluster without external dependencies.

h2. Agent-Based Installer Enhancements

* Extend the existing UI to capture all essential data points (e.g., cluster details, network settings, storage configuration) without requiring YAML files.
* Install without a pre-existing registry in disconnected environment
* Install required operators for virtualization ([OpenShift Virtualization Reference Implementation Guide v1.0.2|https://access.redhat.com/sites/default/files/attachments/openshift_virtualization_reference_implementation_guide_v1.0.2_0.pdf])
* List of Operators:
** OpenShift Virtualization Operator
** Node Health Check (NHC) Operator
** Fence Agents Remediation (FAR) Operator
** Node Maintenance Operator (NMO)
** Loki
** OpenShift Logging Operator
** Cluster Observability Operator(COO)
** MetalLB
** Migration Toolkit for Virtualization (MTV)
** Kube Descheduler Operator
** NUMA Resources Operator
** NMState Operator
** OADP

* Note: we need each operator owner to enable the operator to allow its installation via the installer. We won't block the release due to not having the full list of operators included and they'll be added as required and prioritized with each team.

h1. User experience requirements

The first area of focus is a disconnected environment. We target these environments with the [Agent-Based Installer|https://console.redhat.com/openshift/install/metal/agent-based]. 

The current [docs for installing on disconnected environment |https://docs.openshift.com/container-platform/4.17/installing/installing_with_agent_based_installer/preparing-to-install-with-agent-based-installer.html]are very long and hard to follow.

h2. Generala

* Productization of [OCPSTRAT-1985|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-1985] TP features
** Assisted UI
** Appliance

* Build Release pipeline for generic ISO
* Build Release pipeline for “above-the-sea” UI
* Support for OLM operator

h2. Connected phase

* It will be a new option in the Assisted Installer wizard.
* Selecting the new option, a user will receive a simple wizard leading to a customized ISO download.
* ISO will be generated upfront for each Z-release with the latest version of Day-2 operators:
** Minimum x86_64 architecture

h2. Disconnected phase

* Installation:
** Deploy: SNO, 3-Node with additional workers, Standard Cluster with dedicated control plane nodes
*** Including 4th and 5th control plane node
** Possibility to select operators from the predefined list during the installation process

* Upgrade/update:
** Day-2 upgrade without an external registry will be delivered separately. A customer can upgrade the cluster using InternalReleaseImage CR for switching to an external registr

* Expand the cluster with new nodes (scale out and node failure scenarios)
** Scale out scenarios worker nodes for below deployments:
*** 3-Node with 0..n workers
*** Standard OpenShift cluster with dedicated control plane nodes
** Failure scenarios:
*** Worker node failure
*** Control Plane node failure (minimum - document the manual procedure)
** Adding new nodes without an external registry
* Security:
** Authorisation and authentication of Assisted Service on a rendezvous node
** Admin - AI-UI session protection (HTTPS, credentials to access UI) during a cluster installation

h1. Definition of done

* Functionality described above delivered, tested by QE, and documented.

h1. Open question

* Installation monitoring - Once the rendezvous node is rebooted., it may require several minutes between the rendezvous reboot and when the console is effectively available, and during this “blackout” period, the user will not have any way to detect/spot an eventual issue
* Disaster Recovery

h1. Out of scope

* Shared storage solution which should be provided by a customer

h1. Links:

* [Agent-Installer Installation UI for OpenShift Virtualization - update|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1gPmoOYhCq6ZasXIPkdT_p4_ENEAtUjPcE57P3xrV1SE/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.d5othfg3kle8]
* [Simplified Disconnected Installation|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1oDoGvJprWPXSOzk-pM10B6g2UVZcr6u4xPVqMtDqhig/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.yh2dlzhij6zu]
* This document written by Zane Bitter as the Staff Engineer of this area contains an interactive workflow proposal.

* [PRD Installation UX for OpenShift Virtualization |https://docs.google.com/document/d/1em9AHbAAMvhVYupYBoV7kGzcwLjvN10OKdM-MtuZ2D4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.rla2ip2ik78](and notes from regular meetings)

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Enable Karpenter NodePools to vary their resource limits and provisioning behavior based on time-of-day and day-of-week schedules. Cluster administrators can define time windows during which Karpenter aggressively provisions nodes to meet demand, and off-hours windows where Karpenter constrains or stops provisioning — allowing workloads to queue until capacity is available on reserved/savings-plan instances, or scaling the node fleet to zero for non-production environments.

This eliminates the need for external CronJobs, Lambdas, or scripts that imperatively patch NodePool limits — a pattern that is brittle, fights GitOps reconciliation, and creates operational toil.

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)

h4. Core Requirements

# {{NodePool.spec.schedule}} — New optional field defining one or more time windows with associated resource limits:
{noformat}spec:
  # Default limits (apply when no schedule window is active)
  limits:
    cpu: "0"       # Outside all windows: no provisioning
    memory: "0"
  
  # Scheduled limit overrides
  schedule:
    - name: business-hours
      daysOfWeek: [mon, tue, wed, thu, fri]
      hoursOfDay: "09:00-17:00"
      timezone: America/New_York
      limits:
        cpu: "200"
        memory: "800Gi"
    
    - name: weekend-maintenance
      daysOfWeek: [sat]
      hoursOfDay: "06:00-10:00"
      timezone: America/New_York
      limits:
        cpu: "50"
        memory: "200Gi"
{noformat}
# *Scale-to-zero support:* When the active limit is {{cpu: "0"}}, Karpenter MUST:
#* Stop provisioning new nodes for this NodePool
#* Begin consolidating existing Karpenter-managed nodes (respecting disruption budgets)
#* After consolidation, all Karpenter-managed nodes from this NodePool are removed
#* Workloads are either evicted (if no other capacity) or rescheduled to other NodePools
# *Window transition behavior:*
#* *Window opens (limits increase):* Karpenter immediately evaluates pending pods and provisions nodes up to the new limit. No delay.
#* *Window closes (limits decrease):* Karpenter initiates consolidation of nodes exceeding the new limit, respecting {{disruption.budgets}} and {{gracePeriod}}. Not immediate — graceful.
# *Multiple windows:* Multiple schedule entries can be defined. When windows overlap, the *most permissive limit* wins (union, not intersection). This matches the principle of least surprise — if two windows say "100 CPU" and "200 CPU" overlap, the result is 200 CPU.
# *Default limits (no active window):* When no schedule window is active, {{spec.limits}} (top-level) applies. If {{spec.limits}} is not set and no window is active, the NodePool has no limits (existing behavior — unlimited).
# *Disruption budget interaction:* Scheduled limit reductions trigger consolidation, which respects the existing {{disruption.budgets}} cron schedule. If a disruption budget blocks consolidation during a limit reduction window, nodes may remain beyond the scheduled limit until the disruption budget allows.
# *Status reporting:* {{NodePool.status}} includes:
#* {{activeSchedule: business-hours}} (name of the currently active window)
#* {{effectiveLimits: {cpu: "200", memory: "800Gi"}}} (resolved limits after schedule evaluation)
#* {{nextTransition: 2026-06-02T17:00:00-04:00}} (when the current window closes)
# *Metrics:*
#* {{karpenter_nodepool_schedule_active{nodepool, schedule_name}}} — 1 if window is active, 0 if not
#* {{karpenter_nodepool_schedule_transitions_total{nodepool, schedule_name, direction}}} — counter of window open/close transitions
#* {{karpenter_nodepool_effective_limit{nodepool, resource}}} — current resolved limit after schedule evaluation
# *No schedule defined = existing behavior:* This feature is fully opt-in. NodePools without {{spec.schedule}} behave exactly as they do today.

h3. *Out of Scope*

{color:#676767}_High-level list of items that are out of scope._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

* *Pod-level scheduling* — CronHPA, KEDA, kube-downscaler handle pod scaling. This feature is node-level only.
* *Workload-aware scheduling* — Karpenter already handles demand-based scaling. This feature adds time-based limits, not workload analysis.
* *Cluster start/stop* — AKS-style full cluster shutdown. This feature scales the Karpenter-managed node pool, not the entire cluster.
* *Schedule-based instance type selection* — e.g., "use spot during day, on-demand at night." This could be a future extension but is out of scope for v1.

h3. *Background*

{color:#676767}_Provide any additional context is needed to frame the feature._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

* Karpenter is demand-driven — it provisions nodes when pods are pending and removes them when idle. But many workloads have *predictable time patterns* that demand-based scaling doesn't optimize for:
** *Dev/staging:* Nobody works at 2am. Nodes should be gone.
** *CI/CD:* Build queues are deep during business hours, empty at night. Off-hours bursts waste on-demand spend.
** *GPU training:* Jobs run 9-5. $25/hr GPU instances sit idle 14 hours/day.
** *Financial services:* Trading systems run 7am-6pm. Physical servers are idle the rest.
* The current workaround — external CronJob/Lambda patching NodePool limits

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Bring [5-Spot|https://github.com/finos/5-spot] — the FINOS-incubating, CAPI-native controller for time-based machine scheduling — into the Red Hat OpenShift orbit as a *community-supported, OLM-installable operator*.

5-Spot automatically adds and removes CAPI machines on a cron-like schedule. It is driven by a single CRD ({{ScheduledMachine}}) with day/hour/timezone windows, enabling:

* *Cost optimization* — run expensive bare-metal/GPU capacity only during business hours
* *Stranded capacity harvesting* — use idle DR servers as OpenShift worker nodes during the day, return them before nightly DR windows
* *Predictable scaling* — expand and contract clusters around known workload patterns without CronJob hacks

This is a *deliberately lightweight bet*: community-supported posture (like the proactive node-scaling operator), not full productization.



h3. Goals (aka. Expected User Outcomes)

As a *cluster administrator* , I can:

* Install 5-Spot from OperatorHub and define {{ScheduledMachine}} resources to add capacity during business hours
* Trust that machines are gracefully drained and removed when the schedule window closes
* Harvest idle DR/physical server capacity as OpenShift worker nodes without modifying the DR infrastructure
* Use any CAPI infrastructure provider (Metal3, RemoteMachine, CAPA, CAPZ) with 5-Spot — it is provider-agnostic
* Monitor scheduled machine lifecycle via Prometheus metrics and health probes

h3. Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria)

# 5-Spot controller runs against *generic CAPI* (not OpenShift-specific) — remove any OpenShift-only assumptions from upstream code
# OLM operator bundle created — installable from OperatorHub or custom CatalogSource
# {{ScheduledMachine}} CRD ({{5spot.finos.org/v1alpha1}}) is installed and functional
# Controller creates CAPI {{Machine}} CRs when schedule window opens, drains and deletes when it closes
# Graceful node drain respects PodDisruptionBudgets and configurable {{nodeDrainTimeout}}
# Kill switch ({{killSwitch: true}}) works for emergency immediate removal
# Multi-instance HA via leader election
# Prometheus metrics exposed for scheduled machine lifecycle
# Container image is signed and scannable (OpenVEX/SBOM)
# CI/e2e tests run in operator repo — no dependency on OpenShift CI infrastructure

For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*{color}

|Hosted control planes|yes|

|Connected / Restricted Network|Connected|
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)|x86_x64, ARM (aarch64)|
|Operator compatibility| |

h3. *Use Cases (Optional):*

{color:#676767}_Include use case diagrams, main success scenarios, alternative flow scenarios._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

*UC1: Off Hours Capacity* A bank runs trading applications 7am-6pm ET. 5-Spot provisions 20 bare-metal nodes via Metal3 at 6:45am, drains them by 6:15pm. Overnight, nodes are returned to the DR pool.

*UC2: GPU Training Windows* An ML team runs GPU training jobs 9am-5pm. 5-Spot provisions GPU instances (via CAPA or Metal3) during the window. At 5pm, nodes drain and are removed — saving $25/hr per GPU instance for 14 idle hours.

*UC3: Dev/Staging Scale-to-Zero* A platform team runs dev/staging environments during business hours only. 5-Spot scales the dev cluster's worker pool to zero overnight, saving 100% of compute cost for 14 hours/day.

h3. *Background*

{color:#676767}_Provide any additional context is needed to frame the feature._  {color}{color:#0013de}_Initial completion during Refinement status._{color}

5-Spot originates from [FINOS|https://www.finos.org/] (Fintech Open Source Foundation), built by RBC Capital Markets. It addresses a real gap: CAPI defines machine lifecycle, Karpenter defines demand-based scaling, but *neither handles time-based capacity management for physical infrastructure*.

The "Harvesting Dark Cores" use case — running workloads on idle DR servers during business hours via libvirt CAPI provider + 5-Spot — was the signal that shifted engineering's assessment from "very no" to "this makes sense." Enterprise customers with physical infrastructure constraints (banks, railroads, utilities) can't use cloud burst. They need a CAPI-native path to scheduled capacity.

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Workload identity is a key part of the zero-trust model. The SPIRE project aims to simplify the management and distribution of workload identities in the form of cryptographically verifiable identity documents. There is an increasing interest and uptake in this space within the Cloud native ecosystem.  The goal is to give customers a practical and scalable way to establish trust in a multi-cloud, multi-platform environment. It will strengthen OpenShift’s security capabilities and value-add as organizations harden their security policies. 

Support SPIRE integration with Kessel Operator

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Explore and prototype a SPIRE AI Workload Attestor plugin to enable workload identity for AI-native workloads (agents, MCP servers, tools, model runtimes) using SPIFFE.

The focus of this discovery is to design and build a plugin PoC that derives identity selectors from runtime, artifact, and provenance evidence, and demonstrates SPIFFE identity issuance for these workloads.

Include support considerations for SPIRE operator deployments in edge and disconnected clusters.

h3.  *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

 Build a SPIRE AI Workload Attestor plugin PoC

* Demonstrate identity derivation for AI-native workloads using runtime, artifact, and provenance evidence
* Validate end-to-end flow: workload → SPIRE attestation → SPIFFE ID issuance
* Show how AI-native workloads can be represented as first-class SPIFFE identities
* Evaluate feasibility of supporting edge and disconnected environments
* Provide design recommendations for future productization (not part of this JIRA)

*Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

  

* A SPIRE AI Workload Attestor plugin is implemented as a SPIRE Agent plugin and can be deployed in a test environment
* The plugin successfully derives selectors for at least the following AI workload types:
** agent
** MCP server
** tool or skill
** model runtime
* Selector derivation includes evidence from multiple sources:
** OCI artifact metadata (e.g., image digest, annotations)
** Runtime execution context (e.g., process entrypoint, environment variables – allowlisted)
** AI metadata (e.g., Model Cards, Agent Cards, MCP manifests where available)
* The plugin demonstrates deterministic selector generation (same workload → same selectors across restarts)
* The plugin adheres to SPIRE separation of concerns:
** Attestor only derives selectors
** SPIRE Server performs identity issuance
* SPIRE Server successfully issues SPIFFE IDs based on selectors generated by the plugin
* At least one end-to-end PoC flow is demonstrated:
** Deploy AI workload
** Attestor derives selectors
** SPIRE issues SPIFFE ID
** Identity can be inspected/validated
* The selector model includes:
** Strong identity selectors (e.g., artifact digest, entrypoint digest)
** Semantic selectors (e.g., agent ID, framework, workload kind)
** Clear separation of observability-only signals (not used for identity decisions)
* Optional (stretch): Provenance-aware selectors are demonstrated using signed artifacts or similar mechanisms
* The plugin works in a Kubernetes-based environment (via SPIRE Operator)
* Feasibility is validated for:
** Edge deployments (resource-constrained environments)
** Disconnected/air-gapped environments (no external dependency at runtime)
* Documentation for the PoC includes:
** Plugin setup and configuration
** Example workloads and resulting selectors
** Observed limitations and gaps
* Key findings are captured:
** Gaps in selector coverage or standardization
** Challenges in extracting AI metadata at runtime
** Recommendations for future evolution or productization

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) are a widely adopted abstraction for providing isolated, policy-driven, and routable network environments within cloud platforms. As OpenShift continues to expand into bare metal, private cloud, edge, and multi-cluster deployments, customers increasingly require a similar networking model that provides cloud-like network isolation, connectivity, and operational simplicity.

Today, users attempting to implement VPC-like networking in OpenShift must combine multiple low-level networking primitives, including Cluster User Defined Networks (CUDNs), Cluster Network Configurations (CNCs), RouteAdvertisements, EgressIPs, NetworkPolicies, and other networking constructs. This approach is operationally complex, error-prone, difficult to manage at scale, and lacks a unified operational model.

This feature aims to introduce first-class VPC support within OpenShift Networking, providing a higher-level networking abstraction that delivers isolation, routing, policy management, observability, and multi-cluster extensibility through a single cohesive construct. The goal is to enable users to build cloud-like private networking environments on OpenShift bare metal and private cloud deployments while simplifying operations and improving application portability. The enhancement is motivated by emerging customer use cases requiring isolated tenant networks, distributed applications spanning multiple clusters, and consistent networking policies across deployment locations.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

* Define a first-class VPC networking abstraction for OpenShift.
* Provide a simplified and unified user experience for creating and managing isolated network environments.
* Reduce reliance on manual composition of multiple networking resources to achieve VPC-like behavior.
* Deliver tenant-level network isolation and segmentation.
* Support routing constructs comparable to cloud VPC networking models.
* Enable policy, connectivity, and routing definitions to move with workloads and applications.
* Provide a single operational view of network health and connectivity within a VPC.
* Enable VPC extension across multiple OpenShift clusters.
* Support distributed applications that require consistent networking across cluster boundaries.
* Establish a foundation for future networking capabilities such as route tables, shared services, and advanced traffic controls.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

h4. Functional Requirements

* Users must be able to create and manage VPC resources using Kubernetes-native APIs.
* A VPC must provide isolated address spaces and connectivity domains.
* Workloads within a VPC must communicate without requiring manual networking configuration across underlying OpenShift networking components.
* Network policies must be scoped and enforceable within a VPC.
* Routing behavior must be configurable and observable.
* VPC connectivity must be extendable across multiple OpenShift clusters.
* VPC constructs must integrate with existing OpenShift networking capabilities where appropriate.
* VPC state, health, connectivity, and routing information must be observable through OpenShift tooling and APIs.

h4. Operational Requirements

* Lifecycle management must be declarative and GitOps-friendly.
* The solution must support day-2 operations such as expansion, troubleshooting, and migration.
* Failure domains and operational boundaries must be clearly defined.
* The feature must support OpenShift bare metal environments and be extensible to private cloud deployments.

h4. Non-Functional Requirements

* Minimize operational complexity compared to existing approaches.
* Maintain scalability for large numbers of VPCs, workloads, and routes.
* Avoid introducing significant networking performance degradation.
* Provide a consistent user experience across single-cluster and multi-cluster deployments.

 

*_Anyone reviewing this Feature needs to know which deployment configurations that the Feature will apply to (or not) once it's been completed.  Describe specific needs (or indicate N/A) for each of the following deployment scenarios. For specific configurations that are out-of-scope for a given release, ensure you provide the OCPSTRAT (for the future to be supported configuration) as well._*

|*Deployment considerations*|*List applicable specific needs (N/A = not applicable)*|
|Self-managed, managed, or both| |
|Classic (standalone cluster)| |
|Hosted control planes| |
|Multi node, Compact (three node), or Single node (SNO), or all| |
|Connected / Restricted Network| |
|Architectures, e.g. x86_x64, ARM (aarch64), IBM Power (ppc64le), and IBM Z (s390x)| |
|Operator compatibility| |
|Backport needed (list applicable versions)| |
|UI need (e.g. OpenShift Console, dynamic plugin, OCM)| |
|Other (please specify)| |

h3. *Use Cases (Optional):*

* Tenant Isolation
** A platform administrator creates multiple VPCs to provide isolated networking environments for different business units, development teams, or tenants running on shared OpenShift infrastructure.
* Private Cloud Networking
** An organization deploying OpenShift on bare metal wants cloud-like VPC capabilities without depending on a public cloud provider.
* Multi-Cluster Application Deployment
** A distributed application spans multiple OpenShift clusters and requires consistent addressing, routing, and security policies regardless of cluster location.
* Database Clusters Across Sites
** Applications such as CockroachDB require network connectivity across clusters while maintaining consistent policies and routing semantics.
* Network Operations Simplification
** Administrators want to manage networking through a single VPC abstraction rather than coordinating multiple networking resources and controllers.
* Future Shared Services
** Organizations want to expose shared services such as ingress, egress, DNS, monitoring, or security services to multiple application environments through controlled VPC connectivity models.

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*

* What API objects and CRDs will define a VPC?
* How are VPC boundaries enforced within OpenShift Networking?
* What routing model will be implemented?
* How will route tables be represented and managed?
* How will address management be handled within and across clusters?
* What interoperability requirements exist with existing networking constructs such as UDNs, CUDNs, CNCs, RouteAdvertisements, and EgressIPs?
* How will VPC connectivity be extended between clusters?
* What observability and health reporting mechanisms are required?
* How will VPC lifecycle operations be managed?
* What scalability targets and limits must be supported?
* What migration path will exist for customers using current networking primitives to emulate VPC functionality?
* How will security boundaries and policy enforcement be implemented?

h3. *Out of Scope*

* Full cloud-provider-specific VPC feature parity.
* Replacement of existing OpenShift networking implementations.
* Comprehensive SD-WAN functionality.
* Network virtualization beyond the defined VPC abstraction.
* Advanced network service mesh functionality.
* Full network security platform capabilities beyond VPC-level isolation and policy integration.
* Immediate implementation of all future VPC-related capabilities such as advanced route table management, transit networking, or centralized service networking.
* Changes unrelated to networking isolation, connectivity, routing, or policy management.

h3. *Background*

VPCs have become the standard networking abstraction in public cloud environments, providing isolated networking domains with well-defined routing, connectivity, and security boundaries.

OpenShift customers increasingly deploy workloads in environments that resemble private clouds rather than traditional Kubernetes clusters. These deployments require cloud-like networking constructs while remaining portable across infrastructure providers.

Current OpenShift networking capabilities provide the foundational building blocks necessary to create VPC-like environments; however, achieving a complete solution requires coordinating multiple resources and controllers. This creates operational complexity and increases the likelihood of configuration errors.

The proposed enhancement introduces a higher-level abstraction that simplifies network management while enabling future networking innovation. It also establishes a foundation for multi-cluster networking use cases, which are becoming increasingly important for edge, hybrid cloud, and geographically distributed applications. Multi-cluster networking capabilities are also becoming increasingly relevant across OpenShift networking technologies.

h3. *Customer Considerations*

* Customers should experience a simpler networking model compared to assembling multiple networking primitives.
* Existing networking workflows should remain functional during migration and adoption.
* The feature should reduce operational burden and troubleshooting complexity.
* Customers should gain improved visibility into network health and connectivity.
* Multi-cluster deployments should benefit from consistent networking behavior.
* Documentation and migration guidance will be critical for adoption.
* The feature should align with customer expectations established by public cloud VPC offerings while remaining OpenShift-native.

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

Documentation should include:

* Conceptual overview of OpenShift VPCs.
* Architecture and design principles.
* VPC API specifications and examples.
* VPC lifecycle management procedures.
* Routing and connectivity configuration guidance.
* Multi-cluster deployment patterns.
* Security and policy configuration examples.
* Observability and troubleshooting guidance.
* Migration documentation from existing networking constructs.
* Scalability and operational best practices.
* Day-2 operational procedures.
* Reference architectures for common customer deployment models.

h3. *Interoperability Considerations*

The VPC abstraction must interoperate cleanly with existing OpenShift networking capabilities, including:

* User Defined Networks (UDNs)
* Cluster User Defined Networks (CUDNs)
* Cluster Network Configurations (CNCs)
* RouteAdvertisements
* EgressIPs
* NetworkPolicies
* Ingress and egress networking services
* Existing OpenShift networking operators and controllers

Additional interoperability considerations include:

* Multi-cluster networking frameworks
* GitOps workflows
* OpenShift Virtualization networking requirements
* Hybrid cloud deployment models
* Existing customer networking automation
* Future networking enhancements that build upon the VPC abstraction

The design should minimize disruption to existing deployments while providing a clear path toward adoption of the VPC model.

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

Enable LVMS to support direct EUS-to-EUS upgrade paths for all future long term suport versions (ELC). Starting with OpenShift 4.23 (last EUS version in 4.x)  to OpenShift 5.2 (the first ELC release in the 5.x series), with as few intermediate operator upgrades as possible — ideally zero.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

Per the [OpenShift 5.0 Operator Compatibility Guidance]([https://docs.google.com/document/d/1humaZXIe2yvRA0zjObyMBrIHWDmQXqO_p0SAGD9uX3k|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1humaZXIe2yvRA0zjObyMBrIHWDmQXqO_p0SAGD9uX3k]), all OLM-managed Red Hat operators must provide a supported EUS-to-EUS  upgrade path. Starting with OpenShift 5.2, the gap between EUS releases will be two versions, and control plane nodes will support direct updates skipping up to two intermediate releases. 

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

# LVMS operator version available on OCP 4.22 must have a supported upgrade path directly to an LVMS version on OCP 5.2 (skip-level). 
# Internal Rebase and QE procedures are updated to add same level of testing for all future ELC releases. 
# Validate that no intermediate LVMS operator upgrade is required for the cluster EUS-to-EUS transition.
# Ensure CSV metadata (olm.maxOpenShiftVersion or minKubeVersion ranges) covers the full 4.22 → 5.2 span.
# Handle any Kubernetes API removals between K8s 1.29 (OCP 4.22 baseline) and K8s 1.38+ (anticipated OCP 5.2 baseline).
# Handle any LVMS API changes done in the skipped versions
# Ensure RHCOS 9 and RHCOS 10 worker node compatibility throughout the upgrade.
# Validate no "Resource Not Found" errors for deprecated APIs used by LVMS during the skip-level transition.
# EUS skip-level upgrade test (4.22 → 5.2) passes with LVMS installed: cluster upgrades successfully with a supported LVMS update path.
# No operator downtime or workload disruption during the EUS-to-EUS cluster upgrade.
# LVMS storage provisioning and volume operations remain functional throughout and after the upgrade.

h3. *Questions to Answer (Optional):*

none

h3. *Out of Scope*

None

h3. *Background*

_n/a_

h3. *Customer Considerations*

n/a

h3. *Documentation Considerations*

n/a

h3. *Interoperability Considerations*

n/a

h2. *Feature Overview*

This feature extends the Day-2 compute node addition capabilities introduced in OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) 4.22.z under *OCPSTRAT-2650*. Originally designed to enable the addition of physical bare-metal compute nodes to an existing cluster on Day-2, this enhancement expands the scope to support *Virtual Machines (VMs)* under the exact same operational circumstances and workflows. Control plane nodes are out of scope.



h2. *Goals*

* *Expand Cluster Scaling Flexibility:* Enable cluster administrators to seamlessly add VM-based compute nodes on Day-2 using the same workflows previously restricted to bare metal.
* *Target Environment Parity:* Provide verified support for VMware vSphere environments, ensuring that VMs can act as drop-in alternatives to bare-metal nodes during Day-2 expansion.
* *Target Persona:* *Infrastructure Administrators* and *Cloud Architects* responsible for scaling, managing, and maintaining on-premises cluster capacity.
* *Reference Implementation:* Validate and establish VMs provided by *OpenShift Virtualization* as the preferred and fully tested reference platform, while keeping the underlying mechanism generic enough to accommodate other virtualization platforms. 



h2. *Requirements*

h3. 1. This feature is aligned with [+OCPSTRAT-3312+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-3312] including all requirements/assumptions/limitations.

h3. *2. Quality Engineering (QE) & Validation Requirements*

* *Workflow Parity:* QE must fully validate that the Day-2 node addition workflow designed for bare metal functions successfully when executed with a VM.
* *Target Infrastructure:* Validation must be performed within a *VMware vSphere* environment.
* *Reference Validation Platform:* Testing must prioritize VMs provisioned and managed by *OpenShift Virtualization*, ensuring stability, proper node joining, and correct configuration inheritance.
* *Regression Testing:* Ensure that expanding this workflow to VMs introduces no regressions or stability issues to the existing bare-metal Day-2 addition process.

h3. *3. Documentation Requirements*

* *Documentation Update:* The existing Red Hat OpenShift documentation page for _Adding Bare Metal Nodes_ must be updated to explicitly cover VM-based compute nodes.
* *Procedural Clarity:* Documentation must outline any specific prerequisites or configurations required when substituting a bare-metal node with a VM (e.g., network mapping, resource allocations).
* *Platform Callouts:* Explicitly mention that while VMs provided by OpenShift Virtualization on vSphere represent the preferred and fully tested configuration, the feature is not strictly limited to this platform.

h3. *3. Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Reliability:* The Day-2 VM node joining process must match the stability metrics of the original bare-metal implementation.
* *Maintainability:* Since no new code is written, the existing codebase must remain clean, ensuring that future installer updates treat bare-metal and VM nodes consistently within this workflow.



h2. *User Scenarios*

*As an* Infrastructure Administrator,

*I want to* add a virtual machine as a Day-2 compute node to the existing OpenShift cluster on vSphere/vCenter or VCF.



h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Day-1 Provisioning Updates:* This feature is strictly limited to Day-2 operations (adding compute nodes to an already active, running cluster). Any modifications or validation of Day-1 installation flows are out of scope.
* *New Core Feature Development:* No new APIs, CLI flags, or installer code logic will be developed for this feature request.
* *Non-vSphere Automation Frameworks:* While the underlying workflow may function on other hypervisors, formal QE validation and documentation updates are strictly scoped to VMware vSphere (with a preference for OpenShift Virtualization).



h2. *Links*

h3. *Tracking & Epics*

* *Feature Request (RFE):* [|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-9342][+RFE-9342+|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-9342] _(Extending functionality to VMs)_
* *Base Feature (GA 4.22.z):*[+OCPSTRAT-2650+|https://issues.redhat.com/browse/OCPSTRAT-2650]_(Day-2 Bare Metal compute node addition)_

* *Target Infrastructure:* Validation must be performed within a *VMware vSphere* environment.
* *Reference Validation Platform:* Testing must prioritize VMs provisioned and managed by *OpenShift Virtualization*, ensuring stability, proper node joining, and correct configuration inheritance.
* *Regression Testing:* Ensure that expanding this workflow to VMs introduces no regressions or stability issues to the existing bare-metal Day-2 addition process.

h3. *3. Documentation Requirements*

* *Documentation Update:* The existing Red Hat OpenShift documentation page for _Adding Bare Metal Nodes_ must be updated to explicitly cover VM-based compute nodes.
* *Procedural Clarity:* Documentation must outline any specific prerequisites or configurations required when substituting a bare-metal node with a VM (e.g., network mapping, resource allocations).
* *Platform Callouts:* Explicitly mention that while VMs provided by OpenShift Virtualization on vSphere represent the preferred and fully tested configuration, the feature is not strictly limited to this platform.

h3. *3. Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Reliability:* The Day-2 VM node joining process must match the stability metrics of the original bare-metal implementation.
* *Maintainability:* Since no new code is written, the existing codebase must remain clean, ensuring that future installer updates treat bare-metal and VM nodes consistently within this workflow.



h2. *User Scenarios*

*As an* Infrastructure Administrator,

*I want to* add a virtual machine as a Day-2 compute node to the existing OpenShift cluster on vSphere/vCenter or VCF.



h2. *Out of Scope*

* *Day-1 Provisioning Updates:* This feature is strictly limited to Day-2 operations (adding compute nodes to an already active, running cluster). Any modifications or validation of Day-1 installation flows are out of scope.
* *New Core Feature Development:* No new APIs, CLI flags, or installer code logic will be developed for this feature request.
* *Non-vSphere Automation Frameworks:* While the underlying workflow may function on other hypervisors, formal QE validation and documentation updates are strictly scoped to VMware vSphere (with a preference for OpenShift Virtualization).

h2. *Feature Overview*

This feature allows users to extend an existing OpenShift Container Platform (OCP) cluster on vSphere by adding bare metal compute nodes. This capability enables a hybrid architecture, combining the convenience of a virtualized control plane with the performance and efficiency of bare metal worker nodes. The feature supports clusters installed using Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure (IPI), User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI), and the Assisted Installer, providing a clear path for customers transitioning their workloads from a fully virtualized environment to a hybrid one without requiring a full cluster reinstallation.

h2. *Goals*

The primary goal of this feature is to enable customers to seamlessly integrate bare metal compute nodes into their existing OCP clusters on vSphere. This provides a flexible and scalable solution for workloads that benefit from running on bare metal, such as those with specific hardware requirements or high-performance computing needs.

As a *cluster administrator*, I want to add bare metal compute nodes to my existing OpenShift cluster on vSphere so that I can support workloads on bare metal without reinstalling my entire cluster.

h2. *Requirements*

h3. *Functional Requirements*

* *Node Provisioning*: The system must allow for the addition of new bare metal compute nodes to an existing OCP cluster on vSphere. The provisioning process should be initiated by the cluster administrator.
* *Networking*: The solution must support multiple subnets for the machine network to accommodate bare metal nodes in a hybrid setup.
* *Workload Migration*: The cluster must support the seamless rescheduling of pods from vSphere VM nodes to the newly added bare metal compute nodes.
* *Cluster Upgrade*: The hybrid cluster must support standard OpenShift upgrade procedures. This includes both connected and disconnected environments, utilizing an external registry provided by a customer (for disconnected clusters) or Red Hat repositories (for connected clusters).
* *Node Replacement*: The solution must provide a procedure for replacing a failed bare metal compute node, following standard OpenShift practices.
* [optional] Full automation for the provisioning and decommissioning procedures if possible.

h3. *Non-Functional Requirements*

* *Usability*: The process for adding and managing bare metal nodes should be as straightforward and well-documented as possible for a cluster administrator.
* *Maintainability*: The solution should be integrated with existing OpenShift management tools and procedures to ensure ease of maintenance and troubleshooting.
* *Reliability*: The addition and replacement of nodes must not negatively impact the stability or availability of the existing cluster.
* *Security*: The feature must adhere to existing OpenShift security rules and best practices.

h2. *Use Case*

# A customer has an existing OCP cluster on vSphere, installed using one of the following methods:
## Installer-Provisioned Infrastructure (IPI)
## User-Provisioned Infrastructure (UPI)
## Assisted Installer
## Agent-based Installer
# The customer has an independent the third-party Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver, the vSphere CSI driver is not in use and has been explicitly disabled by the customer by setting `managmentState: Removed` for vSphere CSI driver's ClusterCSIDriver object..
# The customer needs to add bare metal compute nodes to the cluster for new or existing workloads.
# The cluster administrator adds new bare metal compute nodes to the cluster.
# Pods are successfully rescheduled from the original vSphere nodes to the new bare metal nodes.
# The customer is able to perform an in-place upgrade of the hybrid cluster.
# The customer is able to replace a failed bare metal compute node following a documented procedure.

h2. *Scenarios*

h3. *Main Success Scenario: Add, Upgrade, and Replace*

# A cluster administrator adds a new bare metal compute node to their existing OCP on vSphere cluster using a documented provisioning procedure.
# The new bare metal node successfully joins the cluster and is marked as Ready.
# The cluster administrator migrates workloads by rescheduling pods from an existing vSphere VM node to the new bare metal node.
# The cluster administrator removes the now-empty vSphere VM node, completing the decommissioning process.
# The administrator performs a standard OpenShift cluster upgrade, and the hybrid cluster with both vSphere and bare metal nodes upgrades without issue.
# In a separate event, a bare metal compute node fails and needs to be replaced. The cluster administrator follows the standard OpenShift procedure to replace the failed bare metal node with a new one. The new node successfully joins the cluster.

h2. *Out of Scope*

* Support and validation of the native *vSphere Container Storage Interface (CSI) driver* in a hybrid cluster with bare metal nodes.
* Support and validation of any *third-party CSI driver*. While a customer might use a third-party driver in their environment, this feature will not provide specific validation or support for it.

h2. *Links*

* *OpenShift Documentation*: [Installing on vSphere|https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/openshift_container_platform/4.19/html-single/installing_on_vmware_vsphere/index]
* *Richard's spike blog post* [Adding bare metal nodes to platform vSphere|https://hackmd.io/@rtSHzRyKSyCsctnsgdbQwA/S1fu4CJtJx]

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*  

_Functions are implicitly globally unique, currently requiring manual steps to assign DNS.   This has proven to be an unnecessary technical hurdle for new users.  Domain auto-assignment is the defined fix.  Functions are part Infrastructure-as-Code, and to that end, their FQDN is their primary key.  This is a hard requirement for multiple GA features, such as variants and SSL autoprovisioning._

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

When a user chooses a Funciton name, it supports FQDN, restricted by cluster domains configuration, and auto-provisions the SSL certificate (a hitherto manual step).

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

FQDN allowed as Function name.  Autoprovisions routes and ssl.  Works without Knative Serving, KEDA or other autoscaling backend.  Gracefully degrades without CertManager. 

*Notes:*

This is a _decomposition_ of [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2457|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/OCPSTRAT-2457|smart-link] into constituent pieces.  Fields on this issue are therefore set as a mirror of the source issues at time of creatino (labels, assignments, etc).  See [https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SRVOCF-866|https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/SRVOCF-866|smart-link] for notes and philosophy behind this refinement.  Prioritization is left as a deliberate omission to trigger an approval pass.

h3. Feature Overview (aka Goal Summary)

As an OpenShift cluster administrator running self-managed clusters with short-term credentials (AWS STS, Azure Entra Workload ID, GCP Workload Identity), I need an automated, supported mechanism to rotate the bound service account signing (private) key so I can meet PCI-DSS v4 (life-cycle management, req. 8) and NIST key-rotation requirements without downtime.

This is *Phase 2* of the work begun under OCPSTRAT-1727 / OCPSTRAT-1523. Phase 1 delivered a documented manual procedure (CCO-601, {{docs/rotate-oidc-key.md}}, openshift-4.19). Phase 2 automates as much of that procedure as feasible across all three cloud providers.

h3. Goals (expected user outcomes)

Cluster administrators can rotate the OIDC signing key on a regular cadence (at least annually) through a supported, automated workflow rather than a manual runbook. Rotation is seamless for running workloads — older public keys remain in the JWKS to validate previously issued tokens during the overlap window, while new tokens are signed with the new key; pods are recycled gradually as needed with no outage. Applies consistently to AWS STS, Azure Entra Workload ID, and GCP Workload Identity.

h3. Requirements (Acceptance Criteria)

* Automated rotation tooling/workflow (e.g. via {{ccoctl}} and/or CCO) covering AWS, Azure, and GCP.
* Multiple public keys published in the JWKS during the overlap window; configurable retirement of old keys.
* No workload outage during rotation; documented/automated gradual pod recycling where required.
* Updates the OIDC {{.well-known/openid-configuration}} and {{jwks_uri}} artifacts in each provider's object storage.
* Tested and supported; published in official OpenShift product documentation (not only the CCO repo).
* Supports a recurring / at-least-annual rotation cadence.

*Deployment considerations*

||Consideration||Applicability||
|Self-managed / managed / both|Self-managed|
|Classic (standalone)|Classic|
|Hosted control planes|TBD|
|Topology (multi-node / compact / SNO)|All|
|Connected / Restricted Network|All|
|Architectures|x86_64, aarch64|
|Cloud providers|AWS (STS), Azure (Entra Workload ID), GCP (Workload Identity)|
|Backport needed|TBD|
|UI need (Console / OCM)|TBD|

h3. Out of Scope

* Managed offerings (ROSA/ARO/OSD) — TBD, to be assessed separately.
* Manual procedure (already delivered in Phase 1 / CCO-601).

h3. Background

Phase 1 (OCPSTRAT-1727, closed) documented manual rotation for all three providers; broader manual feature OCPSTRAT-1523 (closed, 4.18). Customer *Amadeus IT Group* (RFE-6397, case 03786147) requires automated rotation for PCI-DSS v4 / NIST compliance and has repeatedly requested a tracking Jira for Phase 2 (most recently 2026-06-05). Amadeus also plans GCP-on-WIF deployment and will need the same capability there. Phase 2 should also fold in the 2026 CCO changes flagged by Ju Lim. Related: RFE-1026 (GCP automatic credential rotation, Critical), RFE-4934 (AWS STS key-pair rotation).

h3. PIXAA process notes

* CCO is now under PIXAA; this Feature carries the {{pixaa}} label for prioritization eligibility.
* Product Manager: Marcos Entenza Garcia. Assignee (eng manager), Architect (engineer), and Team (Pod) to be set by PIXAA during Engineering refinement.
* Likely delivery Pod: blue-marlin (CCO — Jeremiah Stuever; manager Sharada Vetsa). Cross-cloud architecture to be taken to the Cloud Provider CCSIG (Theo Barber-Bany / Joel Speed).
* Child Epics/Stories/Spikes to be created by the Assignee + Architect + PM during Engineering refinement (not pre-created here).

h3. Related references

* RFE-6397, OCPSTRAT-1727, OCPSTRAT-1523, CCO-601
* Customer case 03786147 (Amadeus)
* Manual rotation docs: {{github.com/openshift/cloud-credential-operator/blob/master/docs/rotate-oidc-key.md}}

h3. *Feature Overview (aka. Goal Summary)*

This feature aims to ensure that once all Platform Agnostic and Rolling Streams operator teams have completed their TLS consistency/ML-KEM development and per-component testing, the resulting cluster (sum of all parts) does indeed behave as intended: TLS 1.3 with hybrid ML-KEM being the default offered key encapsulation protocol. This applies to all TLS servers of all operators *and all operands* — it is not sufficient to validate operator endpoints alone.

h3. *Goals (aka. expected user outcomes)*

A newly deployed OCP 5.0 cluster should use quantum-safe key encapsulation by default for all TLS connections served by Platform Agnostic and Rolling Streams operators *and their operands*.

h3. *Requirements (aka. Acceptance Criteria):*

Once an OCP 5.0 cluster is up and running, a CI job can scan all discoverable service endpoints exposed by Platform Agnostic and Rolling Streams operators *and their operands* to ensure they're using TLS 1.3 (required for PQC support), and then run a series of smoke tests to validate basic functionality while in PQC-mode.

h3. *Testing Approaches*

Teams should validate ML-KEM support using one or more of these approaches:

# *Cluster-wide scan* - tls-scanner periodic CI covers basic cluster installation
